speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the doors of the house were opened to the public you led us in the usual prayer for our beloved sovereign, Queen Elizabeth. Today the people of Canada are celebrating officially the anniversary of Her Majesty's birthday. In this house, as in other years, we will be evidencing our devotion to Her Majesty by continuing to give consideration to the public business of her Canadian subjects. But with your permission the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and I would like to suggest that before doing so we stand and sing together the first verse of the royal anthem.

speechtext:
This point has to do with clause 4. I should like to ask the minister whether he would give some consideration to adding the province of Saskatchewan to the province of Alberta as therein provided. The clause reads:
Where an employee is usually employed in the Yukon Territory or in the Northwest Territories, he shall for the purposes of this act be deemed to be usually employed in the province of Alberta.
Great developments are taking place in the Northwest Territories immediately north of the northern boundary of Saskatchewan, and there will be further developments in the near future. Those developments being contiguous to the province of Saskatchewan, should any proceedings be taken in respect of compensation to a person entitled under the act, provision should also be made for the right of that person to have it regarded, for the purposes of this act, that he be employed in the province of Saskatchewan. I do not think any of the territories are north of the province of Manitoba, but if they are the province of Manitoba should be included as well.
I suggest that is in keeping with the developments that have taken place in the territories. A few years ago these developments were exclusively in the areas of the Northwest Territories contiguous to the northern boundary line of Alberta. Today, however, with the developments taking place in the Northwest Territories directly adjacent to the northern boundary of Saskatchewan, I ask the minister whether he would not consider adding the province of Saskatchewan in that section.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
This will become clause 5 if the amendment is passed, but perhaps you would permit me, Mr. Chairman, to answer my hon. friend on the point he has just made. I can tell him no representations were made to the standing committee on industrial relations with regard to the province of Saskatchewan with respect to compensation applicants from the Northwest Territories. I admit that strong representations were made on behalf of the province of British Columbia. But when consideration was given to all the factors it did seem to my department that a more expeditious carrying out of these applications could be done for the present at least through the province of Alberta. I can assure members from British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Manitoba that if as we go forward it appears there are advantages to be gained by having it done in several provinces rather than


in one, I will certainly give full consideration, to the matter if I am minister of labour, but I do not think it would be useful to doit at the present time.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Would the minister explain why it is more expeditious for a person coming within the ambit of the act and working immediately north of the northern boundary of Saskatchewan, for example, to be deemed to be employed in the province of Alberta? As I recollect the statistics I have seen, at least half of those employed are from the province of Saskatchewan. Why should those people, for the purpose of so-called convenience, be deemed to be employed in the province of Alberta? I can understand section 5 very well. It states:
Where an employee, other than a person locally engaged outside Canada, Is usually employed outside Canada he shall for the purposes of this act be deemed to be usually employed in the province of Ontario.
I can understand the reason for not having a multiplicity of loci for employment purposes, but I cannot understand why there should be this concentration of development in the Northwest Territories into the province of Alberta. I feel this is happening not only in connection with the matter before us now but with regard to other matters. I think the minister might give consideration to the request, which in my opinion is reasonable. Certainly the experience in the last couple of years of those of us who live in Saskatchewan has been that there is a continuing channelling of the development in the Northwest Territories and also in northwestern Saskatchewan into Alberta.
I believe this is not an unreasonable request. Certainly an equal number, if not most, of the employees in the areas north of Saskatchewan are from Saskatchewan, and there is no justification whatever for deeming them to be usually employed in the province of Alberta. I know that practically all the developments taking place in northern Saskatchewan, and even in Saskatchewan as a whole, are being by-passed in favour of developments in the city of Edmonton and the province of Alberta. While that city is represented in the government by a minister who is concerned with northern development, nevertheless we in Saskatchewan believe- and believe fairly, I suggest

that we have a right to consideration; and that area of northern Canada which will become greater as the years go by should not, by legislation or otherwise, be channelled into any one direction, namely in the direction of the city of Edmonton.

Government Employees Compensation Act
When I make this statement I am expressing a view held generally in Saskatchewan, without regard to party considerations. We believe these developments contiguous to our province should not be considered as the monopoly or the right of a province not contiguous to the areas in question.
At the moment I am not considering an amendment, but I do feel that the minister's argument, when he says it would be more expeditious for a person north of Saskatchewan to have to go into Alberta to have his claim considered under the compensation laws there provided for government employees, has behind it an explanation other than the convenience of the individual. I would ask the minister to explain how it is considered there would be any added convenience for an employee in the area north of Saskatchewan, where major developments are now taking place, to do as he has suggested. I would ask him to tell the committee why it would be more convenient that such person be subject to the law of Alberta, as a resident of that province would be.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on this same subject-and I am speaking with a view to obtaining information rather than of making a statement-I understood the minister to say that the procedure he has suggested would be more expeditious. I understood him to say that both the Northwest Territories and the Yukon would be considered in this instance as coming under the workmen's compensation act in Alberta.
I cannot understand why this should be so, and I am asking the minister for some enlargement of his earlier statement. The Yukon is north of British Columbia. All the systems of transportation to the Yukon go through British Columbia, either along the Alaska highway, or by the air lines from Fort St. John. Therefore I suggest that, from the standpoint of operating with expedition, communication by transportation passes through British Columbia either by road or by air.
Then in addition I believe the workmen's compensation act in British Columbia is just about the best to be found anywhere in Canada. I suggest, therefore, that from the standpoint of expedition and equity in the matter of transportation, and from the standpoint of the excellence of British Columbia workmen's compensation legislation, these claims should be handled by the province that is closest. I fail completely to understand the statement by the Minister of Labour, and I hope he will explain not only what he means but how his department came to the conclusion he has indicated today.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to support the hon. member for Prince Albert and the hon. member for Vancouver East. I can see no reason why Alberta should be selected for the purpose indicated. I do not know what the minister will think of my suggestion, but I am wondering why the section should not read in this way:
Where an employee, other than a person locally engaged outside Canada, is usually employed outside Canada, he shall for the purposes of this act be deemed to be usually employed in the province immediately south of his location in the Northwest Territories.
I do not see why any one province should be picked out in this instance. And I certainly agree with some other statements made by the hon. member for Prince Albert in this connection. If we are going to select any province I cannot see any better argument for selecting Alberta than there would be for the selection of any other province, including Saskatchewan.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this matter is
of importance, of course, but I wish to point out that it will have no importance in the development of the province in which these claims are handled.
During 1954-55 we have had in the Northwest Territories a total of 294 claims, 156 of which required only local medical aid. Since I brought in the amendment before- and, by the way, this is not a new amendment; it is just a carrying forward of existing procedure-the matter has been very thoroughly worked out with the government of the Northwest Territories and with the department of government here in Ottawa responsible for their administration.
There were a number of factors to be considered. For instance, the ordinances of the Yukon and of the Northwest Territories are based upon Alberta rates. It is basic, of course, to this legislation that the benefits be similar to those available to workers in the same area. If one were to take the relatively small number of accidents that occur among federal government employees in the northwest country and were to have the employees of some companies claiming in British Columbia, others in Alberta and others in Saskatchewan, I am quite sure it would make for more delay than if they were to be done through one channel.
It is not necessary, of course, for an applicant to travel to make his claim. He can make it where the accident takes place. The experience we have had and the discussions which have taken place in the committee would indicate that at least for the present the suggested procedure would be in the best interests of the claimant. It is not because of the benefit to the administration, but

Government Employees Compensation Act rather because we can give better service to the claimant who suffers an accident and submits a claim on account of that accident.

speechtext:
I do not wish to hold up this
legislation, but I would ask the minister to explain why he considers this is for the benefit of the claimant. What is the advantage for the claimant who is injured in the Yukon or in the Northwest Territories when his application must go through Alberta? I agree with the minister when he says there is no advantage to any province that handles these cases, because the federal government reimburses that province only to the extent of the actual expenditures and a share of the administration costs, in accordance with the amount of work that has to be done. Actually it is an added burden on a province; therefore I am looking at it only from the point of view of the person who is injured. From that point of view, and that alone, I maintain that in the interests of the claimants they should be permitted to go to that province that can give them the best return. And I say, with all due respect to Alberta and Saskatchewan, that British Columbia can do that. Where is the advantage to the claimant who must go through Alberta, and not through Saskatchewan or British Columbia?

subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I can give that at once. If the legislation required that the applicant should go through the province immediately to the south, British Columbia, Alberta or Saskatchewan, it would be necessary to take a map of the Northwest Territories and say that those who are working within certain limits shall go to Saskatchewan, and none other. Those who are working in those limits shall go to Alberta, and none other. I can visualize prospectors flying over the Northwest Territories, not knowing when they pass those imaginary lines. It would be a very great deal of work to undertake for a very small amount of employee compensation work involved.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Where do prospectors come in under this act?

subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION

speechtext:
Perhaps the minister can explain the difference between the workmen's compensation acts in the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba? Is there any difference between the acts? If so, in what particular; for in determining the matter of expedition I do not think the minister answers the criticism when he says that after all there are not going to 

be many cases. Everyone will join with him in the hope for a minimum of accidents. Why do you choose the province of Alberta? Has it a better workmen's compensation act than the other provinces? Can the minister say in what particular the act is better? If the act is not better, there is no serious difficulty in the way of altering the section to read, "in the province directly south of the place where the accident has taken place", or words to that effect.
The minister said you would need a map. Well, that is not very difficult. You know what the parallels are. If it is within a certain parallel, then it is the province of Saskatchewan; if it is within another parallel it is the province of Alberta, or the province of British Columbia. I repeat, this is another example of what we in the province of Saskatchewan most definitely resent, namely the concentration of developments in the northern parts of Canada adjacent to our province which are more and more forcibly, and under legislation and direction, finding their way from our province into the province of Alberta.

speechtext:
Apparently the minister himself had some doubts as to the efficacy of his rule of thumb, for I see that under clause 10 a substitution is to be made. A little later the following provision is to be made:
Subject to the approval of the governor in council, the minister may make regulations for-determining, for the purpose of this act, the place where an employee is usually employed . . .

Why is the minister, by order in council, to have the power to override clause 4, which provides that the employee shall be deemed to be usually employed in the province of Alberta? Clause 10 provides that the minister may make regulations tor determining, for the purpose of this act, the place where the employee is usually employed. Why does the minister ask for the power in a later clause to override the absolute powers of clause 4?
Possibly he can explain that at this time. It might clarify the reasons for clause 4; for it seems strange to me that in one section of the act provision is made that such and such a province shall be deemed to be the place where an employee is usually employed, and then another section provides that the governor in council may, by order in council, make regulations for determining, for the purposes of this act, the place where an employee is usually employed. To me that does not seem to make sense. Why the definite provision in one section, and in a later amended section the provision that the governor in council may himself alter the express words of a statute?
That is another power we did not object to at the time, but it is certainly a most unusual thing to say in one section that a person shall be deemed to be resident within a certain province as far as the application of the act is concerned, and then in another section that the minister, through the governor in council, whatever the actual words of the statute may be, may change them at his whim for any reason. I cannot understand why there should be any insistence on the provision that for the purposes of this act the person shall be deemed to be usually employed in the province of Alberta. Why is it so necessary to make explicit reference to the particular province unless there is some purpose in mind?
Expedition does not appeal to me, which is the argument the minister put forward. It is equally expeditious whatever the western province may be. I suggest that the Alberta compensation act is believed by his departmental officials or himself to be a more effective or efficient act than the acts of the other provinces. If that is the reason, then let us have the information. It will clarify the matter a great deal.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
The clarification of the expression "usually employed" in the discussions of the standing committee had no particular relation to the item which is now before us, namely the matter affecting the Northwest Territories. It was felt by the committee that there might need to be a clarification of that
Government Employees Compensation Act expression "usually employed" as it appears in various places in the bill. In order that this might be done, whether the accident took place within Canada or whether it took place in another part of the world with respect to a Canadian civil servant, there should be authority to make a clarification, if it should be necessary; but it has nothing particularly to do with this matter of the Northwest Territories.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
I still have one more question to ask the minister, because I think it is only right that hon. members should have a clarification of what is meant and what the plans of the department are. In my day I have had a good deal to do with many hundreds of workmen's compensation cases. I can see some of the problems under this section. If the section goes through the way it is now and a person is injured in the Yukon or in the Northwest Territories, will he be considered as coming under the compensation act of the province of Alberta? What are the particulars the department has worked out in the case of a person injured in the Northwest Territories who becomes either a total disability case or a permanent partial disability case?
I am certain the minister must know that if an injury occurs in a certain province, or in this case in a territory, it would have to go through the province, but the home of that person may be somewhere else. He may be on partial disability or total disability, and then he would come under the compensation laws of that province, in this case the province of Alberta.
If his home were in British Columbia-and I imagine as far as the territories are concerned there must be quite a few who consider their homes to be in that province-if further medical examination or attention were required, or if there were to be an adjustment in the degree of disability, then the board of that province could function only with the authorization of the workmen's compensation board of Alberta.
Although the number of injuries that might occur in the Northwest Territories or the Yukon would likely be small, I would imagine the majority of those concerned would not be residents of Alberta. I think we should hear from the minister whether consideration has been given to that phase of the problem, and what determination has been arrived at as to how these cases can be handled. Is the situation to remain as it is now, so that no matter whether a man is a TD or PPD he will have to go through the province of Alberta in order to obtain any adjustment in the way of medical attention or hospitalization?

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if my hon. friend will look up certain portions of the proceedings of the committee-I will send him the page numbers-I think he will find a complete reply to his question. Under the old act, if a man were injured in the Northwest Territories he came under the laws of Alberta regardless of where his home base was. The intention of this bill is to provide that federal government employees working in the Northwest Territories or the Yukon who are injured will come under the laws of the province in which the federal department establishment under which they are employed is located.
If an official from Ottawa who is on a department establishment here proceeds to the Northwest Territories and meets with an accident, he will receive compensation under the Ontario laws. The same thing would hold true if he were a federal civil servant who proceeded from Vancouver or Victoria to the Yukon and met with an accident. The man injured would come under the laws of the province in which he was usually employed, in that case British Columbia.
There was a long discussion in the committee because there was some fear that there might be a misunderstanding of the phrase "usually employed". The minister was given the right to work out regulations to cover that point. If a government employee was usually employed and had his base in Saskatchewan and was injured while working in the Northwest Territories, he would come under the provisions of the Saskatchewan law. Only those working under establishments or in federal offices located within the Northwest Territories come under this special dispensation applying to Alberta.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few observations at this time, mainly as a result of the very illuminating evidence we heard the other day in the fisheries committee. For the benefit of those who may not be as familiar with the situation as those of us who heard that evidence, may I say it was revealed that as a result of the lamprey menace in the great lakes the trout fishing in lake Huron is now completely ruined. That industry was valued at $5 million a year, was engaged in by both Canada and the United States, and has now practically disappeared. The federal department of fisheries in conjunction with the corresponding department of the United States

Great Lakes Fisheries
are now making a joint effort to stamp out the lamprey menace and put the fishing industry of the great lakes back on a paying basis.
It is unfortunate that this action was not taken years ago, because the trout fishermen are suffering a heavy annual loss, and until the industry is restored in that area the loss will continue. I am glad to see the Minister of Finance in his seat, because he has never been too far away from the great lakes, and would be more familiar than most with what is taking place there. Under the convention -the two senior governments are going to undertake this joint effort, which had been carried on previously by eight states in the United States and by Ontario in Canada.
The evidence in committee disclosed that weirs have been constructed in creeks and streams up which the lamprey have gone to spawn. The evidence disclosed that in their last year the lampreys grow from a length of four or five inches to 18 inches, having fed mainly on trout. It is when they go up to spawn that the challenge is placed before the two departments concerned. What alarms me is that the situation had reached a point where it was almost beyond immediate control by any department, simply because research work was not undertaken years ago when it was learned that the lamprey was becoming a curse to the fishing industry. With the situation today, even if all the eels going up to spawn are caught it will still be seven years before the evil can be stamped out.
We find in the estimates for the Department of Fisheries, under item 145, a vote of $355,000 to provide for the share of this federal government in the administrative expenses of the great lakes fisheries research committee established jointly with Ontario. This sum is also to provide for a program designed to eliminate lampreys in the great lakes.
Evidence in the committee disclosed that $50,000 a year has been set aside for research work, part of this sum to be paid by Ontario and part by the dominion. No doubt a greater sum will be paid by the agencies in the United States because, after all is said and done, one of the great lakes, namely lake Michigan, is in their country. Lake Michigan has been infested with this curse to the same extent that lake Huron has, so I would assume that in due course they would pay more than we ought to pay. It appears that the program calls for work to be done in lake Superior, to hold the line at the more southerly end of that lake where it empties into the lower lakes. I agree that this is sound business. I do not agree that no attempt should be

made to eliminate this curse in lake Huron and re-establish the fishing industry there on a sound basis.
It appears that there are some 50 streams in the north channel of lake Huron up which these lampreys go to spawn, and apparently these are the only streams up which they go. That in itself is important. I was worried for fear that they were spawning all over in the different streams of the different lakes. They told us in the committee that these weirs or contraptions they have for destroying the lamprey cost anywhere from $5,000 to $10,000, depending on the proximity to accessible roads and that sort of thing. That would be the cost in lake Superior.
It has not been my practice at any time since I have been a member of this house to ask any department of government to spend money just for the sake of pleasing somebody who thinks it should be spent. Here is an industry that is very important to a great many people. It needs to be invigorated. I am going to make a suggestion to the minister in the hope that he can persuade his colleagues on the front benches to accept it. I hope it meets with his approval because, after all is said and done, if one part of our national economy is disturbed or crucified to the extent of $5 million annually it affects the whole economy.
I know the minister would be only too anxious to re-establish the trout industry without delay. It cannot be done overnight. I am very glad this action is to be taken without further delay. While the scientists do not claim to have perfected a device to completely destroy the lamprey, they are working on different projects. As a matter of fact one of the witnesses suggested that through some electrical means, or sound waves, they might be able to exterminate the lamprey without injuring any other fish.
I said these weirs or contraptions cost anywhere from $5,000 to $10,000. I am going to suggest that the minister place in the supplementary estimates an amount sufficient to take care of weirs on these 48 or 50 streams where they know probably 90 per cent or even more of the lamprey go to spawn. We all agree that the attack must be made in lake Superior to hold the line. But let us at the same time re-establish the fishing industry in the other great lakes, particularly the trout industry.
One may say that the fishing industry in the great lakes is greater in poundage and in dollars and cents than it has been in the past. I admit that. A great many fishermen are fishing oftener and are using more nets and greater efficiency as time goes by than

they did years ago; but I am going to tell the minister this. I said it before when I made a few remarks on this subject. In my part of lake Huron the fishermen are going broke. Some of them have been using up their surplus. One fisherman I have in mind has a terrific overhead. He is a very capable fisherman. Because of the lamprey and other things that affect the fishing industry he has been operating in the red to such an extent that he cannot continue any longer.
I urge that we rehabilitate the trout industry in lake Huron, and at the same time hold the line in lake Superior. It is going to be a seven-year job before it will be completed. With the greater knowledge these scientists have and will be obtaining, the problem will be licked. It is just too bad it was not tackled years ago. If the area is not too remote and is accessible by boat, the department can complete work on the 48 or 50 weirs with the amount that is being immediately provided, and then they can work in lake Huron; but the work will not be done at a cost of less than $200,000, and that amount will have to be spent yearly until this curse is eliminated.
I would suggest-and I hope the minister will agree with me-that we might better spend $250,000 or $500,000 a year to remove this curse and save an industry that produces $5 million a year. That sounds like common sense. I hope the members of the treasury board and the members of the cabinet will agree with this suggestion. Let us not wait for five years to spend $250,000, when we can do it today. It is too bad the department did not start 10 or 15 years ago when they knew the curse existed.
When the figures were given the other day they disclosed that we produced almost 15 times the amount of trout five years ago that we produced last year or the year before. It was quite apparent to some that something ought to be done. I make no apology for saying this. The responsibility should have been accepted, no matter what government was in power. Research is not new. They knew what was going on. They had been experimenting for some years on methods to eliminate this curse. .Those methods should have been proceeded with at great haste. I would ask the government to appropriate an extra $250,000 or $500,000 a year to re-establish this $5 million industry.
The lamprey are now preying on the trout. After the trout are gone they will turn to the whitefish. The lamprey will be found not only in lake Huron but in all the other lakes as well. I sincerely hope the government will agree to the suggestion. I think the sum of $50,000 for research is picayune.
Great Lakes Fisheries
That is the amount to be expended by the federal and provincial governments. What is needed is $100,000, $200,000 or $500,000 a year. That is needed to prevent the loss of $5 million. That is not pin money. These fishermen work hard to earn what they make. They make a great contribution to our economy.
As I said earlier, I never make it a practice, and I do not intend ever to make it a practice, to ask for moneys unless I think they can be wisely spent. I do not know of an instance where this government could spend money more wisely than in an effort to destroy this pest and at the same time re-establish the fishermen.
I suggested the other day in committee, and I would like to put it on the record here, that in conjunction with this program of eliminating the lamprey eels in these streams off the north channel the government at the same time should restock the lower end of lake Huron, that is near Sarnia, with trout fingerlings. The minister indicated in committee the other day that they were working in full accord with the Ontario government, and I am sure that if arrangements could be made to restock this area these fish would gradually find their way along both shores. I suggest also that this be a co-operative effort with the level of government with which you are dealing on the other side.
Perhaps next year when the estimates are being considered and it is found that these contrivances are not as successful as it is hoped they will be, sufficient money will be voted for research so we can do our part in re-establishing the fishing industry on the great lakes.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO IMPLEMENT CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES SIGNED SEPTEMBER
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was interested in listening to the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, because he spoke most sensibly and realistically. The fishermen along the shores of lake Superior are appreciative of this legislation. Men make their living from this industry in places such as Heron Bay, Marathon, Terrace Bay, Schreiber, Rossport, Nipigon, Port Arthur and Fort William. These men tell me the fish are getting scarcer. I should like to ask the minister if compensation could be arranged for the catching of these lamprey eels. Such compensation would be attractive to the younger element among fishermen.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO IMPLEMENT CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES SIGNED SEPTEMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, coming as I do from British Columbia I may not have the same direct and immediate interest in this question as the hon. members who have preceded me, but I do want to say that I found the evidence given before the committee in connection with this bill most interesting and

Great Lakes Fisheries informative. I think everything possible should be done to accelerate the program being initiated by this legislation.
I gathered from the research experts who appeared before the committee that they are hopeful they have devised a method of dealing with the mature lampreys as they enter the streams to spawn, but I gathered also that they are not quite so certain the methods they are considering to deal with the lamprey before it reaches maturity have reached the point where they can be assured that these lampreys can be disposed of at that stage. It seems to me if it should be found that further appropriations for research would expedite the efforts to deal with the lamprey in the earlier stages, and thus get around the necessity of having to wait for six and seven years, it would be a worth-while expenditure.
This bill proposes to ratify an international treaty arrangement. Just how effectively this will work out will depend a great deal upon the attitude taken by the United States counterparts to the Canadian members of the international commission to be set up. I feel it would be appropriate for this parliament to indicate that there is a desire on the part of Canada that everything possible be done to accelerate this program and restore the fisheries in lakes Huron and Michigan. But I would suggest that before the minister brings an increased appropriation before parliament he should ascertain through this international commission that the United States people are prepared to do their share. Then any increased appropriation by us would be worth while. Otherwise it might be throwing good Canadian dollars down the drain, or I suppose one could say letting them run over Niagara falls.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO IMPLEMENT CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES SIGNED SEPTEMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure we are all aware of the importance of the fishing industry to the economy of Canada. The report of the Department of Fisheries for 1953 indicates that for that year the total catch was approximately 1-8 billion pounds; the income of the fishermen amounted to $91-8 million, and the catch had a market value of $179 million. When we look at the matter from that point of view we can readily understand the importance of this industry to the national economy, as well as its tremendous importance to a great number of our population who must depend upon the industry for a livelihood.
When introducing this measure the minister referred to other international commissions which had been set up, such as the international Pacific halibut commission, the Pacific salmon fisheries commission and others. I am sure these different treaties have commendable objectives and in the 

main are achieving the desired results, but we do not agree with all the regulations which have been passed in order to accomplish those objectives.
It may seem a little strange that members from British Columbia should wish to speak on Bill No. 279, to implement a convention on great lakes fisheries; but in view of the importance of fisheries to our economy I should like to make two or three observations. The bill would appear to have two main purposes, research and lamprey control. This was a very interesting subject which came up for debate in the committee. I must confess my ignorance of the lamprey situation. In fact, I had not heard about it until it was brought to our attention by the minister in his introductory remarks. But after seeing the film that was shown on the occasion of the committee's meeting, and also hearing the departmental officials as they outlined the problem, it certainly indicates a very serious situation existing in the great lakes. I am sure that this measure that has been introduced will be very welcome to every member of the house, and of course, doubly so to the fishermen who are concerned. Therefore, I should just like to indicate, Mr. Chairman, that we are supporting this bill, and we hope that the efforts that are being put forth to control the lamprey menace and also develop the interests of the fisheries in the great lakes will be successful. Therefore we in this group welcome and support the bill.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO IMPLEMENT CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES SIGNED SEPTEMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am very grateful to the hon. members who have spoken in approval of the substance of this bill. I do not think there is any need for me to make any lengthy remarks at the present time. I spoke at some length at the resolution stage of the bill. My parliamentary assistant went into it in some detail on the second reading of the bill, and when we were before the committee on marine and fisheries we had before us two top scientists of our department, specialists in freshwater fisheries, whose evidence I know was found to be of very great interest to members of the committee. The committee reported back the bill with no amendments, but with the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Lambton West that perhaps we should be doing more on this.
I should perhaps just answer one or two of the points that have been made here. The question was asked why we had not gone into this problem earlier. The administration of the great lakes fisheries is not under the federal Department of Fisheries but under the province of Ontario. The province had been concerned for some time about the

depredations of the sea lamprey. For those of you who are from the inland provinces, the sea lamprey is a member of one of the lower orders of eels whose normal habitat is the sea and which comes into rivers to spawn. Many years ago the lamprey came up the St. Lawrence and were able to change their environment to the extent that they lived in lake Ontario without returning to the sea and spawned in the streams flowing into lake Ontario. They have been there for some years and have not done too much damage there. However, they passed through the locks around Niagara and entered lake Erie and lake Huron. They did little damage in lake Erie, because the streams flowing into lake Erie come through flat ground not suitable for spawning. However, in lake Huron and lake Superior they have found river conditions ideal for spawning and so have become a great problem. The lamprey must go upstream to spawn in the spring of the year, just after the break-up. The male and female lamprey lay and fertilize the eggs, from 60,000 to 100,000 eggs per female, which hatch out during the summer. The small lampreys drift down to a mudbank and lie there four years burrowed in the mud. In the fifth year they come down to the lake and begin their destructive activities.
In that one year, as the hon. member for Lambton West reminds us, they increase in length from four inches to 18 inches, feeding entirely on the blood and body juices of other fish, the principal victim being the lake trout, a most valuable fish. The whole great lakes fisheries are very valuable, both in the size and the species of catch. The fact that this lake is in the centre of a great populated area cuts down the difficult problem for fisheries of the transportation of fish. The difficulty in the province of Ontario was in trying to handle this problem by itself, since across lake Superior there are eight states similarly affected by the different fisheries regulations. There was obviously not much point in the province of Ontario launching a large-scale lamprey control program if nothing was done across the lake, because population of lamprey move back and forth.
In 1946 the federal government was asked by the province to take action, and since that time we have been negotiating with the federal government of the United States to try to bring about an international agreement similar to the very successful ones we have on the east and west coasts. The one difficulty with the United States government was not lack of willingness, because their fishermen have been more affected than ours; it was the lack of federal jurisdiction. In the American states the primary jurisdiction over fisheries rests 50433-254
Great Lakes Fisheries
with the state governments. However, the United States government was able to work out a plan acceptable to the states and a bill is before congress at the present time to approve this treaty. When this bill is approved by parliament and congress, the commission can begin its work.
In our estimates last year, when we saw it was likely that this commission would be approved, we had an item of $150,000 for lamprey control and $15,000 for research, to begin control by our department. We spent $161,000 of that last year. It is always difficult to get a program like that under way and, of course, we have no federal fisheries officers in the great lakes area. This year we have raised that vote to $330,000, which is the amount our scientists and engineers tell us can be usefully spent this year. We have increased our research vote also. We are putting up $25,000, and the province of Ontario is matching that. This is all in anticipation of the work of the commission. It is true that we are concentrating our lamprey work on lake Superior. I think there is good reason for that. The lamprey is just now entering lake Superior, and we think we can stop that entry now by concentrating our attack there and so saving the lake Superior fisheries. The next step, having learned the methods which are most satisfactory, will be to move back into lake Huron. It will be a long process, because the lamprey has a seven-year cycle. The most effective way to kill it is as it is going into the stream to spawn, which happens only once in a cycle. But we are also engaged in the poisoning of the mudbeds in which the small lamprey lives for four years, which will cut down the incidence of lamprey even in the intervening years. I do not think there is too much point in trying to restock lake Huron until we have substantially cut down the lamprey population for I do not think we should be restocking the lake for the lamprey to feed upon. The hon. member for Lambton West has pointed out that there is a loss of $5 million a year in the commercial catch of lake trout as a result of the depredations of lamprey. That is true for that species but there has been one offsetting factor. As the population of lake trout fell off, populations of other fish have increased because the food used by the lake trout became available to them. The result has been that, despite the lamprey, the value of the total catch of all species has not declined very much. We consider that the job of this commission is to provide the scientific knowledge for what we call scientific management and control of the fisheries to restore the balance between the lake trout
4018	HOUSE OF
Great Lakes Fisheries
and the other commercial fish. Lamprey control is only one aspect of that scientific control.
The hon. member for Fort William asked if there was any commercial value to the lamprey. Unfortunately, there is not. There is a small market among some Europeans for smoked lamprey. The lamprey is a very low form of fish; it has cartilage instead of bone and is not even a good eel. It is very difficult to catch in the lake because it does not feed on any bait except live fish. As far as next year's budget is concerned, that of course will be recommended to parliament and to congress by the commission when it is set up. I may say that I heartily agree with the hon. member for Lambton West that Canada has received good value for what this parliament has spent on the work of these international fisheries commissions. Last year's increase in the catch of salmon and halibut paid for the costs of these commissions many times over.
You will notice that in the convention attached to the bill provision is made for the division of costs by the commission. The reason for that is that these fisheries are of more importance to the United States than they are to Canada, for one reason. We share Ontario, Erie, St. Clair, Huron and Superior, but the states have lake Michigan entirely to themselves. Therefore they have more at stake. It may be therefore that the division of costs will be a little bit heavier burden on the states than on ourselves. I thank the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and the hon. member for Fraser Valley for their remarks. Our province of British Columbia is a long way from the great lakes, but we are the people who have seen the value of such treaties and what they can do to restore fisheries which were apparently on the way out. Our scientists are convinced that by this co-operative work with the federal government of the United States and the province of Ontario and the eight states across the way, we can restore the great lakes fisheries.

speechtext: Will the minister answer a question? Have you considered giving a bonus or compensation to anybody who catches these eels?

speechtext: These lampreys are there by the million. They are worthless but we are spending money killing them where they are most vulnerable.

speechtext: Shall the clause carry?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO IMPLEMENT CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES SIGNED SEPTEMBER
speechtext:
The point I attempted to make, Mr. Chairman, was that the department not only hold the line in


lake Superior, but that they do something more this year, not wait until next year or the year after. I think they should do something this year when they know that they have some 50 streams running into the north channel. It is not as though they are all over lake Huron. They are there probably within 50 or 60 miles. I think that an effort could be made this year to kill these lampreys when they go up to spawn. If it is too late to do anything this year, maybe preparations could be made so that something could be done next year. My argument is that there is no occasion for delay. You are now tackling the problem. I say that you should accelerate that attack.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO IMPLEMENT CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES SIGNED SEPTEMBER
speechtext: May I again point out that the vote we have today is really on an interim basis in anticipation of the establishment of the commission. We hope the commission will start its work this summer. We have done the necessary engineering to spend effectively this $330,000 on weirs and electrical fences in the present year. I am sure when the commission makes its first report we shall be able to do the engineering work to take care of any larger program they may recommend. At the moment I agree with our officials who say that the most important work should be in lake Superior, to kill them there and then to move back into lake Huron and lake Ontario.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO IMPLEMENT CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES SIGNED SEPTEMBER
speechtext:
But, Mr. Chairman, when it comes to the matter of dollars and cents, your officials spoke of the matter the other day. They are highly qualified men and I am certainly one of the members of that committee who was glad to hear their evidence. They said that these weirs which are built on these streams or tributaries to the lake would vary in cost from $5,000 to $10,000 depending on the accessibility to highways, boats or that sort of thing. Here in the north channel you certainly have accessibility by boat. There is no question about that fact. I see the minister who represents that particular area sitting in his seat. I am going to suggest that he read what has been said today and what was said a few days previously.
After all is said and done, I agree-and I have said this before-that you should make your attack in lake Superior where you know you are going to meet with success because they have only been in there recently. You know where they are spawning. You also know that these cursed things come up about 50 streams running into lake Huron and in that north channel. It is not as though you had to wander all around lake Huron. Why hesitate to spend a quarter of a million

dollars this year? Unless you do spend it you are going to continue to lose $5 million worth of trout a year from these lakes; that is not only for us but I mean for the United States. Half of that should be our portion. Unless that money is spent you are not going to kill the lampreys in lake Huron. You are not going to re-establish the trout fishing in lake Huron. In all seriousness I suggest that this is a common ordinary dollar-and-cent proposition where you invest $100,000 or $250,000 or half of that and your return is probably $1 million or $2 million a year. There is no man with common sense who will disagree that that is a good economic policy for you to follow. After all, you are not going to stamp out the curse of the lamprey eels in lake Huron by killing them up in lake Superior. They are still going to exist in lake Huron. After they take your lake trout, the next thing will be the whitefish. In all seriousness I suggest that an effort be made to accelerate the attack by including lake Huron in your program.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 2 agreed to.
On clause 3-Convention approved.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO IMPLEMENT CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES SIGNED SEPTEMBER
speechtext:
I wish to speak for a moment on clause 3. I did not speak on clause 1 because I made it plain at another stage of the proceedings that this party was heartily in favour of this act. But clause 3 brings in the convention itself. I was interested in what the minister said a few moments ago and I was wondering whether he could amplify that for the benefit of this committee. I do not think this matter was raised before. At least it was not dealt with in detail as far as I know in the special committee to which this matter was referred.
As the minister pointed out, the great difficulty in dealing with this thing in the past has been the question of jurisdiction. You have at least eight American states on the south of the great lakes and you have the province of Ontario on this side. As to the constitutional question, as I recall the constitution the American states have the residuary powers and the American congress have the specially delegated ones. The reverse is the situation in so far as Canada is concerned or at least that is the situation today under the decisions and so on and so forth.
Just what is the position in so far as these American states are concerned? Have they delegated their authority to the American congress? And if so, how? Right now, of course, everyone is frightened. Everyone is prepared to co-operate. But suppose that five or six years from now the situation is 50433-254J
Great Lakes Fisheries
relatively under control and then we will say the state of Michigan passes regulations which are contrary to the regulations which may be passed by this commission. Would that state or any other state be in a position to do so or have they, either by legislation, by contract or in any manner delegated their authority to the American congress so that the Dominion of Canada knows that they are dealing with the duly authorized authority? In one of the articles of the convention, namely article 10, we find this provision:
Nothing in this convention shall be construed as preventing any of the states of the United States of America bordering on the Great Lakes or, subject to their constitutional arrangements, Canada or the province of Ontario from making or enforcing laws . . .
And so on. The convention is obviously drawing a line of distinction-at least that is suggested by article 10-as between Canada and Ontario on the one hand and the American states on the other. I would ask the minister to clear up that point for the benefit of the committee.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO IMPLEMENT CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES SIGNED SEPTEMBER
speechtext: There is no jurisdictional problem in Canada about any of these treaties because the federal government has control over the fisheries. The province of Ontario is our agent in the control of sport fishing and the great lakes fisheries. As far as the American states are concerned, our legal officers were concerned about this matter and have looked at the arrangements made now. These American states have agreed to give the federal government the necessary authority for this period of 10 years. The commission is just for 10 years, and then is subject to renewal to be worked out.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO IMPLEMENT CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES SIGNED SEPTEMBER
speechtext: How have they agreed?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO IMPLEMENT CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES SIGNED SEPTEMBER
speechtext: I am sorry, but not being a lawyer I cannot answer that question. But it was to the satisfaction of our law officers. We have a parallel situation with regard to the international salmon commission on the west coast. The American waters are in the state of Washington which has control over fishing there and that state has given the necessary authority to their federal government now for the last 18 years. The arrangement is most satisfactory as far as regulations are concerned.

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport) moved
subsubtopic: AUTHORIZA- TION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 351, respecting Canadian National Railways.

subsubtopic: AUTHORIZA- TION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext: Is the minister going to make a statement?

subsubtopic: AUTHORIZA- TION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I pointed out when introducing the bill, its primary purpose is to consolidate into one statute the legislative provisions relating to Canadian National Railways. A complete enumeration of these legislative provisions is set forth in the second schedule of the bill. This schedule shows that there are no less than 23 enactments that are to be repealed in whole or in part. As this means that at the present time each of these 23 statutes must be consulted in order to determine the exact provisions of what I may call the charter of the Canadian National Railways, I am sure that no further arguments than this are needed in order to persuade hon. members of the desirability of consolidating all of these provisions into a single statute.
In examining the bill it will be found that, though in some instances the wording in some sections has been altered to conform to modern standards of drafting, only five changes in the enactments applying to the company are made. Three of these are intended to give the company (1) power to operate a telecommunication system; (2) power to construct short branch lines, and (3) power to operate motor vehicles for the carriage of traffic. The fourth change is being


made so as to authorize officers and employees of the company to act as directors of partially owned subsidiaries; and, finally, the last change is the setting up of a simple procedure to extinguish the charters of constituent corporations.
Some of the subsidiaries of Canadian National already possess powers to operate telecommunication facilities and motor vehicles, but it is considered that it would be more convenient if these powers were vested in the parent company itself. I should like to say a few words further to that subject at the end of these remarks.
I should now like to say something with regard to what I have described as short branch lines. As will be noted from the text of the bill itself, section 183 of the Railway Act, which permits railway companies in general "to construct, maintain and operate branch lines not exceeding in any one case six miles in length", is not applicable to Canadian National Railways. The powers of the company to construct railway lines are to be found in section 20 of the Canadian National Railways Act which empowers the company to construct railway lines, branches and extensions, etc., in respect of the construction of which parliament may authorize the necessary expenditure or the guarantee of an issue of the company's securities. In simpler words, this means that the company may not undertake the construction of branch lines or extensions, even though they are less than six miles in length, until the necessary expenditure for the specific branch line or extension has been approved by parliament. It happens not infrequently during the interval between annual budgets that the management of the Canadian National Railways receives applications from industries for short spur lines to serve their plants; and I think that it obviously is desirable that the railway should be in a position to respond to these applications and build the required trackage as quickly as possible.
It is proposed, therefore, to give the company the power to construct railway lines, branches and extensions which do not exceed six miles in length, and so to put it in a position comparable to that of the railway companies governed by section 183 of the Railway Act to which I referred a moment ago. As in the past, however, the decision to construct such line, branch or extension will remain subject to approval by the governor in council, and it will still be necessary that its location be sanctioned by the Minister of Transport. Having regard to the fact that all other railways in Canada governed by the Railway Act may, subject to that legislation, proceed with the construction of branch lines

and extensions not exceeding six miles in length without parliamentary approval, I think it would be timely to free the Canadian National Railways from the disability affecting it and endeavour to place it on a footing similar to that of its competitors.
Under existing legislation, section 8 (3) of the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act, only directors of the Canadian National may represent the company on the board of directors of any partially owned company. For reasons of greater convenience it is proposed to authorize not only the directors but also officers or employees of the parent company to serve on boards of directors of these partially controlled companies.
With respect to the extinguishing of the charters of constituent corporations, I may say that there is no provision in the statutes for the surrender of a charter of a railway company which is usually incorporated by special act and it is, therefore, necessary to obtain an act of parliament. As will be seen from the first schedule of the bill, the Canadian National Railways system comprises a large number of constituent companies. It is hoped that the setting up of a simple procedure to extinguish the charters of constituent corporations will facilitate the steps now being taken by the management to simplify as much as possible the corporate organization of the railway.
I wish to assure hon. members that this bill is the result of long and careful study by the management of the railway, the various government departments concerned and the cabinet. After second reading of the bill, if it is the pleasure of the house to adopt it, I shall propose that the bill be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. Officials of the company will be in attendance at the committee to explain the various provisions of the proposed legislation.
I should like to add a particular word with regard to the apprehension which appears to exist in the minds of persons engaged in the operation of trucks and buses on highways that it was intended by this legislation to enable Canadian National Railways to enter competitively the field of highway and bus transportation. I think that what I said in the discussion of the resolution should perhaps have set aside any doubts as to the intention of the government on that score in presenting this legislation, but on rereading one or two sections of the bill I think it may be found that they might lend themselves to an interpretation that there was the intention on the part of the government to
Canadian National Railways give very broad powers to Canadian National Railways with regard to highway transportation when such is not the case.
During the discussion of the resolution I said, in explaining this particular power in the bill, that the railways in the past had been under the disability that at times, when consideration has been given to the abandonment of a short line, the railway has been in the rather peculiar position before the board of transport commissioners of being unable to offer, on behalf of the railway company itself, to undertake to provide motor service in lieu of a passenger train. They have had to produce the undertaking of some subsidiary to provide that service. They have no power to operate motor vehicles, so that they are unable to give a formal undertaking that they will establish a motor service as an alternative to the train service that they propose to abandon.
As I said then, Mr. Speaker, it is not intended there should be any change of policy with regard to the powers of the railway so far as highway transportation is concerned. However, it does seem that section 18 of the bill might lend itself to the interpretation that all of the companies enumerated in the first schedule of the bill were declared works for the general advantage of Canada. I think it will be necessary to make amendments to the bill when it is in committee in order to avoid giving to the railways broader powers than we have in mind.
From an examination of the list of companies appearing in the first schedule to the bill, particularly part III, where there are a large number of companies mentioned, it will be seen that it is clearly an error in drafting that has led to the impression that it was the intention of the government to declare as works for the general advantage of Canada, for example, the operation of a company called Canadian National Railways (France) or Central Vermont Transit Corporation.
I think if that list is examined carefully it will be found that perhaps the reason for the present disquiet with regard to this policy in highway operations arises from the fact that Canadian National Transportation, Limited, is included in these companies in part III. It is my intention, therefore, to avoid any doubt, to move that the act be amended so as to exclude, as works for the general advantage of Canada, the operations of the companies mentioned in part III of the schedule to which I have referred.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian National Railways, through its company, Canadian National Transportation, Limited, has very comprehensive highway powers; but it is not intended
4022	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways to give such comprehensive powers to the Canadian National Railways. As will be found by reference to the bill, it is intended only that the parent company shall have powers in conjunction with or substitution for a rail service. This is designed primarily in order to regularize the pickup and delivery services in the metropolitan centres, and to give the company corporate powers to enable it to provide trucking or bus services in cases in which rail line abandonment would not be permitted by the board of transport commissioners unless a formal undertaking with regard to road transport were submitted.
As I said earlier the primary purpose of the bill is to consolidate a large number of enactments relating to the Canadian National Railways. I have no doubt that for that reason the bill will commend itself to the house, and I think it will be found that the other changes are in the interests of the Canadian National Railways.

speechtext: Then it was with particular reference to Canadian National Transportation, Limited, that the minister spoke in making the remarks he did about withdrawing them from the application of clause 18.
