subsubtopic: AUTHORIZA- TION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext:
But clause 27 is one which confers upon the railway company the rights already referred to by the minister, when he mentions that the company may, in conjunction with, or in substitution for the rail services under their management or control, buy, sell, or lease motor vehicles of all kinds and maintain and operate motor vehicles on highways in Canada or elsewhere for the carriage of traffic, and may charge tolls therefor.
Mr. Chairman, this is not a subject that can be disposed of by a removal of the list of companies from the names of those set forth in part III of the first schedule, so that it will not have application to section 18. What section 27 clearly does is to make it possible for the railway companies to organize, in conjunction with or in substitution for rail services, services by motor vehicles.
That may be desirable. There are many cases where I feel sure that there would be agreement that, in substitution for a short line over a difficult route, it might be highly desirable and convenient to provide such service. It may be debatable, it may be arguable, that it is desirable that the railway company should have power to engage in long-range trucking and in long-range passenger service by motor vehicles, or in other activities of that kind.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the bill as it is now drafted places no limitation upon the powers of the railway company to enter into that field. That brings us back to certain matters that were before the house last year. It will be recalled that, after long years of litigation, there was a case from New Brunswick which was carried to the Supreme Court of Canada and from the Supreme Court of Canada to the privy council. That case is reported in the Law Reports (1954) Appeal Cases, page 541, and is the case of Attorney General for Ontario and others, appellants, and Israel Winner (doing business under the name and style of Mackenzie Coach Lines) and others, respondents.
In that case the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada was reversed. It was declared that interprovincial transportation fell within the jurisdiction of the federal government.
Then, having obtained this result, for which very large sums of public money had been spent during litigation that extended over some considerable time, the government completely changed its attitude. Having obtained the judgment it sought, it then proposed to do the very opposite. And we find reported at page 4196 of Hansard for April 28, 1954, the brief statement of the then minister of transport in regard to a conference which

had just taken place at that time. This brief statement by the minister of transport at that time sets forth exactly the position that was taken by this government after it had obtained a judgment of the privy council, which places the full authority over intraprovincial traffic of this kind which they had sought for some time. These are the words of the then minister of transport:
The federal-provincial conference on highway transportation convened in Ottawa on Monday of this week and completed its business this morning. I think it is safe to say that the conference was a successful one.
In view of the position of the federal government that it was reluctant to enter the field of extra-provincial highway transportation, it suggested to the provinces that they control and regulate such extra-provincial undertakings in the same manner as that in which they were controlling intra-provincial movements. The provinces seemed to be willing to accept this suggestion. Thereafter there was drafted a bill which was submitted to the conference for its approval. Dependent upon the reaction of the various provincial governments to this draft bill, the federal government will be willing to give consideration to enacting at this session of parliament legislation which would make the proposed bill valid.
That bill was introduced during the session. It was assented to on June 26, 1954. It was known as the Motor Vehicle Transport Act. I must confess that there seems to be a form of special simplicity that is an inherited quality of ministers of transport. The minister of transport said last year:
The provinces seemed to be willing to accept this suggestion.
Why would they not? They had been fighting this case through the courts for years. They had carried it to the privy council; they had lost. Then, when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) had succeeded in obtaining a judgment from the privy council, which he regards so lightly, he then came back here and, having reported the case to his colleague, the minister of transport, the minister of transport decided that they did not want what the decision gave them, and so they offered to hand this control back to the provinces, and the provinces seemed to be willing to accept this suggestion, according to the minister of transport. But there was a joker, as there is so often, in the measure put forward and enacted as the Motor Vehicle Transport Act, which purported to place under the provincial authorities the issuing of licences and the control generally. We find under section 3, the governing section in regard to the operation of transport, the following:
(3) (1) Where in any province a licence is by the law of the province required for the operation of a local undertaking, no person shall operate an extra-provincial undertaking in that province unless he holds a licence issued under the authority of this act.
Canadian National Railways
(2) The provincial transport board in each province may in its discretion issue a licence to a person to operate an extra-provincial undertaking into or through the province upon the like terms and conditions and in the like manner as if the extra-provincial undertaking operated in the province were a local undertaking.
Then we find in section 5 this important provision.
The governor in council may exempt any person or the whole or any part of an extra-provincial undertaking or any extra-provincial transport from all or any of the provisions of this act.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am not pointing out here for the first time what the effect of that was, because this is what I said when this measure was before the house last year. I am referring to page 5940 of Hansard of June 14 of last year:
The truth is that under clause 5 the whole of this bill can be swept aside by order in council at any time. If it is important that this bill be now put into effect, it is equally important that this legislation remain in effect until parliament has been consulted in regard to the matter, unless there are some reasons which have not been placed before us for the extremely wide power which would be conferred upon the government by the adopting of the measure as it stands.
This is an important subject, Mr. Speaker. This is a subject which is of interest to Canadians generally. In this tremendous country of ours, with its expanding development, transportation by rail, by highway, air or water is all part and parcel of that dramatic development which is now taking place.
Surely it is appropriate that we should assure the most effective type of legislation we can have when we are called upon to deal with any aspect of this great problem of transportation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, when I made that observation I was urging that the bill go before the standing committee. That was not done. I moved at that time that the second reading should not be proceeded with but that the bill should be referred to the standing committee. There was another reason why that should not have been dealt with at that time, and there is a reason why this bill should not be dealt with now. In April of last year there had been a conference of governments of Canada. That conference had been told that this government wanted the control of all intra-provincial as well as extra-provincial transportation to remain under the control of the provincial governments and under their licences. If that is so, then that applies to all transportation by motor vehicle. Anything else would render provisions of this kind utterly meaningless.
If any railway is to be given power to enter that field under a federal law, and that federal law is to override, as it must, if it is within the constitution, a provincial measure, then the situation would simply be that by indirection this government would once again be invading the provincial field, in spite of the

Canadian National Railways fact that it had purported to consult them in regard to a matter of this kind.
There is a very important principle at stake here. There is a principle at stake which has been discussed in this house before. This government goes through the motions of calling a conference of the provincial governments. Then it places something before them. The provincial governments go home thinking that they understand what this government intends to do, and after they go home satisfied with what was told them so reliably they find that by some indirect method this government invades the very field that they said they were not going to invade. That is exactly the proposition before us in this field.
The Minister of Transport had this to say when the motion providing for the introduction of this measure was before the house on April 26 of this year, as reported at page 3198 of Hansard:
There is no intention on the part of the government, in adding to the powers of the railway that of owning and operating motor vehicles, to make any sinister change of policy. We merely intend to make a change which will enable the railways, in effect, to do through the parent company what they have been doing already through subsidiary companies.
Then there was certain discussion, and an interjection in the debate, and the present minister went on as follows:
I do not think it would be an infringement, Mr. Chairman. I believe it is competent for parliament to empower a federal corporation to operate motor vehicles. I do not believe, for instance, that merely because the power is derived from parliament the operator of the motor vehicles could claim he would not be subject to the laws of the province in the operation of those vehicles. I think my hon. friend could find many examples of dominion corporations operating motor vehicles strictly in conformity with provincial requirements.
There is the old axiom qui s'excuse, s'accuse. The very fact that the minister was so emphatic that there was no sinister purpose indicated the fact that at least the purpose could be open to question. There was perhaps ground for apprehension in the loose draftsmanship, but such change as he has indicated he proposes to make in committee certainly would do nothing to remove that apprehension as to the powers conferred by section 27.
I do not believe that it is necessary for the declaration in section 18 to be applicable to any of these operations to make section 27 fully operative. That I submit is particularly so in view of the closing words of the section. Not only does it confer upon the railway company the right to operate in conjunction with or in substitution for the rail services under their management, or control certain motor vehicle operations, it states that they may charge tolls therefor. If

they are permitted by a dominion statute to charge tolls, then surely the operation of tolls is being conferred by this dominion act. If the act relating to the railways is within the competence of the parliament of Canada, then it would override provincial legislation. If there was any question about its overriding provincial legislation, the government could always refer to section 5 of the Motor Vehicle Transport Act, which provides that by order in council they can negative the effect of the act anyway.
The experience of hon. members of this house has surely not been such that we have any reason to doubt that the government would use section 5 of the Motor Vehicle Transport Act if it found any difficulty in permitting the Canadian National Railways to operate this service.
Let us just see where this goes. If this right is given to the Canadian National Railways, is that an indication that the government is going to do the same kind of thing it does with regard to the C.B.C. and give to the government-chosen agency rights which deny fair competition as between private enterprise and government agencies? If so, then it must confer the same right on the Canadian Pacific.

subsubtopic: AUTHORIZA- TION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext: They have it.

subsubtopic: AUTHORIZA- TION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext:
As a matter of fact I was going to say that they have it anyway. If this power is given to one railway, what about the Ontario Northland railway and what about the other railways right across Canada from British Columbia to Newfoundland? Every one of those can then demand, and with justice, equality of competitive position with the Canadian National Railways. You will have broken wide apart the principle enunciated last year in this house by the Minister of Transport when he told the members of the house what they had decided on at the conference of governments. You will be once again repudiating a clear understanding between this government and the provincial governments arrived at at a conference of that kind.
By the procedure being followed in this case you have another of those indirect methods of breaking an implicit understanding between governments which has been repeated over and over again in other legislation. I submit that this bill contains an important principle, a principle which relates to the undertaking upon which the Motor Vehicle Transport Act was introduced. They had their judgment giving them authority; they then purported to confer upon the provincial governments the supervision and licensing of motor vehicle transport. They

come forward now with an amendment to the general act covering the Canadian National Railways which would change the position they took at that time, which would repudiate the position they took at that time, and then they would be able to protect anything that was done under section 5 which can vitiate the whole effect of the Motor Vehicle Transport Act.
I submit that before this bill is proceeded with there should be another conference with the provincial governments. I submit that it is an honourable obligation of this government to call together the representatives of the provincial governments and discuss the effect of section 27 of the act now before us and find out whether that was what was contemplated at the time the governments met last year, and whether that would be a satisfactory arrangement.
I submit that anything short of that would be a dishonourable course in the face of the understanding which was placed before the house last year. It was no doubt made on the expectation that the provinces were to retain the licensing power, the establishment of rates and everything else; but this act specifically states that the railways shall set tolls. Presumably that in turn would come before the transport board. This is not the sort of thing that should be brought before the house in this way.
In the deliberate delay in order to justify the course they were following they brought the motor vehicle transport bill in last year in June at a time when it was not a practical possibility to follow the regular course and submit it to the standing committee. The bill went through the house over our objections as to the procedure being followed. We now have a new device. I do not know whether the government has decided that it was wrong in abandoning the rights it had obtained under the judgment of the privy council; we do not know the whole story, for the whole story has not been told this house.
But whether we have the whole story or not, I submit that, in view of the fact that this government on its own initiative consulted the provincial governments last year, this measure should not proceed until they again consult the provincial governments in regard to the effect of this section. I say that because this section goes far beyond any mere consolidation of the act which we have under consideration. As a matter of fact I question very much if this should have been brought in in this way, because it is a provision far from a mere consolidation of existing statutes. It introduces a completely new principle in regard to the operation of the railways.
Canadian National Railways
I do not wish to be misinterpreted in regard to this. In what I am saying at this time I am not presenting arguments as to the desirability of this right being conferred upon the railways or otherwise. I think every hon. member here wants to see the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian Pacific Railway and every other railway in this country in a position to give the most efficient, the most economical and the most progressive type of service to the people that it possibly can. Within our constitutional authority and within our honourable obligations to the provinces, where an undertaking explicit or implied has been given, then I think that the hon. members of this house will be found ready and willing to confer such rights as will improve the opportunities of the railways to perform the kind of services they do on behalf of the people of Canada.
We must remember of course that trucking and bus services are also a large part of the transportation system of Canada, just as are the air and boat services. The point that I am making is that this privy council decision in regard to the operation of motor vehicles was given in accordance with the government's wish and following the argument of the Canadian government, and they then turned around and purported to hand back to the provinces the very rights they had gained by the privy council judgment, subject to the joker clause in section 5. But the fact remains that the intention was clear, as stated by the minister of transport last year in the statement that I have read to this house, which was made here on April 28, 1954.
I am not going to move an amendment at this point because I hope that the Minister of Transport, confronted with the statement made by the minister who was minister of transport last year, on April 28, will recognize that there certainly would be a failure to carry out a reasonable understanding with the provinces when they proceeded to force through this house by the government majority a section which would challenge the very clear understanding that the provinces had when they met this government last year.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: AUTHORIZA- TION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the voice that I have today, I shall not be imposing on this house for very long. That is almost an invitation for some of my friends in the house to express pleasure that I have a bad cold, but I notice that their kindness and courtesy keep them from doing that.
Mr. Speaker, I shall not comment at any length on the phase of the matter which has been opened up by the Leader of the Opposition. It seems to me that if the government

Canadian National Railways is in any difficulty over this matter, it arises not from the section of the bill that is now before the house but rather from the course that was followed last year when the government sought to get out from under an obligation imposed on it as a result of a court decision. We shall be glad to study all the various angles of this matter, but we shall bear in mind in particular the fact that the chief competitor of the Canadian National Railways is in some instances in the truck and bus business. We do not feel that obstacles should be put in the way of the Canadian National Railways having the same opportunity which is now enjoyed by the Canadian Pacific Railway.
There are just one or two other things on which I wish to make a comment. First of all, I confess to an interest in the legal and constitutional aspects of legislation of this kind. 1 suppose that, as I am a novice in this field, my interest is sharper than might otherwise be the case. I notice in particular the long list of ancient enactments which are to be repealed in whole or in part by the bill the minister is now presenting to parliament. I was interested particularly in the fact that one of these enactments which is to be repealed in part is a statute which was passed before July 1, 1867. It always intrigues me how we can amend legislation which the parliament of Canada did not even enact, even as it intrigues me that we now find it possible in the parliament of Canada to amend the British North America Act even though it was passed in another jurisdiction. Perhaps the very mention of that right gives the answer as to how pre-confederation statutes can be amended. I suppose that in the long run it is the crown which is doing the enacting and if the crown's advisers or parliaments change from time to time it is still possible to do this sort of thing.
One of the pieces of legislation being repealed by this bill is section 3 of chapter 37 of the statutes of 1852, which was entitled "an act to incorporate the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada". I have in my hand a copy of the statutes of the province of Canada passed in the sixteenth year of the reign of Her Majesty Queen Victoria and in the first session of the fourth parliament of Canada. It is an ancient and musty volume. As a printer I enjoy looking it over and realizing that it was all set by hand. A very good job was done by my fellow tradesmen of that day, considering the difficulties of setting type by hand. However, there is this interesting section of this ancient statute, a

statute passed before Canada came into being in 1867, which we are now repealing. It reads as follows:
III. And be it enacted, that the gauge of the said railway shall be five feet six inches: and the fare or charge for each first class passenger by any train on the said railway, shall not exceed two pence currency for each mile travelled, the fare or charge for each second class passenger by any train on the said railway shall not exceed one penny and one half penny currency for each mile travelled and the fare or charge for each third class passenger by any train on the said railway, shall not exceed one penny currency for each mile travelled; and that at least one train having in it third class carriages shall run every day throughout the length of the line.
This particular railway, according to the preamble or clause 1-they are one and the same in this statute-was to run from the city of Toronto to the city of Kingston and thence to the city of Montreal. Obviously, it is time that a section, if it is still the law of the land, that prescribes a gauge of five feet six inches for the railway running from Toronto to Montreal, were repealed. I ask what has happened through the intervening years. Has the railway running on that line been breaking the law, because it has been running on a gauge less than five feet six inches in width? If the government feels it is now necessary to repeal this archaic section, are not some of the other sections in the same statute equally archaic? For an obvious reason I am not going to take the time of the house to read some of the other archaic sections, but I suggest that there are a number that are quite out of date. If it is now found necessary-and I confess it intrigues and puzzles me as to why it should be necessary-to meddle with legislation that was passed before there was a dominion of Canada as we now know it, what about some other statutes that were passed at that same time? There was the Cobourg and Peterborough railway; there was the Toronto and Guelph railway; there was the Galt and Guelph railway; there was the Grand Junction railway; there was the Hamilton and Toronto railway. These are all in this same volume of statutes of 1852. Incidentally, I find that in all of these statutes that I have checked, the provision for a gauge of five feet six inches is spelled out. That is not now the gauge, so far as any of these railways are concerned. Yet those sections in these other acts are not being repealed. The Fort Erie and Goderich line and the Montreal-New York Railway system are also mentioned. The next one I notice is the Quebec Temperance hall association-but that is not a railway. I would ask the minister if he could explain why it was found necessary

to pick out for repeal that one section of the many statutes in respect to railways passed by the old province of Canada; yet apparently it was not found necessary to deal with any other sections of the many statutes in respect to railways passed prior to July 1, 1867.
Now, Mr. Speaker, as I have indicated, it is not my intention to speak at any length. There is really just one other matter to which I shall refer, and I shall do it in a very brief manner simply by reading to the house a letter which came to me shortly after our debate on the resolution preceding this bill. I may say that, if the house wishes to have the signature to this letter placed on the record, I have the authority of the writer of the letter to indicate who sent it to me. I note Mr. Speaker, that you wish me to give the name, and I shall do so. The letter reads as follows:
79 Dunraven Avenue. Winnipeg 8, Man.,
April 28/55.
Dear Sir:-
This letter was addressed to me.
-At this time, when there is so much discussion in the commons about the C.N. Railways, I thought you should know what happened to my husband.
He was laid off effective November 17/54. Hast week he received a 'phone call asking if he was available for work with the railway. He was working at the time at a low rate of pay and so *decided to go back to the railway to better ourselves financially and also because of six years' time spent in the railway service.
On April 23rd he was told to report to Transcona shops on Monday, April 25th. He quit the job he had, returned to the railway and at 3 o'clock the same day, Monday, April 25th, he was given a letter stating he would be through on April 29th due to a "reduction in staff". Eight men were hired and three were let out. Incidentally, I never heard of Donald Gordon taking a cut in salary to help their so-called economy drive.
Yours truly,
(Mrs.) J. B. Johnstone.
Mr. Speaker, on this occasion I do not think I need to make a speech on employment matters so far as the C.N.R. is concerned. That letter speaks volumes. It is a common practice in these days, in speaking of a certain "ism" with which we are having to struggle in the world, to refer to it as being Godless. I ask you, what is more Godless than treating men like that?

subsubtopic: AUTHORIZA- TION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on this measure. I was much interested in hearing what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) had to say with regard to this particular bill which is before the house. A slight reference was made to it by the Conservative party when the resolution was
Canadian National Railways before the house. I was pleased indeed when I heard the Leader of the Opposition speak in much stronger terms. I was not at all surprised, though, to note the stand which was taken by the C.C.F. party when they said they were in favour of Bill No. 351 as it stands, because that would only be extending the power which the C.N.R. seeks so as to equal that which other railways enjoy. The thought came to my mind that maybe it is wrong to have the C.P.R. enjoy such privileges and that two wrongs would certainly not make a right.
Before I go too far with what I intended to say, Mr. Speaker, I want to refer more particularly to what was said the other night. When the resolution was before the house, I was much concerned about this bill particularly when I saw reference made to motor transport. I guess I must be a little bit suspicious when it comes to that subject, because I have been dealing with it ever since 1937 when the agreed charges legislation started in this house and in 1938 when that legislation was passed. The other day when this resolution was before the house I went to some lengths to elicit some information from the minister in charge of it. Briefly I just want to review that discussion in order to show the point that I am going to raise. In the debate on April 26 of this year, as reported at page 3195 of Hansard a reference was made to this matter by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra who had this to say:
The second question has to do with the sentence which says that the C.N.R. is to be given power to operate motor vehicles. I understood from the minister last night that the company is already operating motor vehicles through a subsidiary company, but will he give a further explanation as to whether there is to be any change in the C.N.R. policy of operating motor vehicles?
That was all that he said on that occasion about it. I know he was concerned about it because those remarks show some concern. Then the Leader of the Opposition today went considerably further in expressing the importance of this proposed bill and his alarm over it. It seems, Mr. Speaker, that on the part of this government there is a tendency- whether or not it is intentional, I am not in a position to say, although I think probably it is intentional-of always trying to centralize power in Ottawa and of attempting to infringe upon the rights of the provinces. I shall exemplify that point a little bit further. I want to say at once that I do not believe that is the minister's purpose. When we were in committee discussing railway matters and agreed charges, Mr. Donald Gordon, who is president of the C.N.R., did not make any

Canadian National Railways bones at all about his position with regard to motor transport. He made it quite clear that they were out to do everything they could to get rid of their competitors as far as transport problems are concerned. There was no secret about that. Hence when I saw in this bill the provision for motor transport, I was alarmed, and rightly so, because we in western Canada know what it means whenever the railways propose an increase in freight rates, supposedly, as they say, because of truck competition. It is we, the ones who are in the non-competitive areas, who get soaked by the increase. Therefore we must be ever alert to that invasion of our rights. When this question was before the house I put this question briefly to the minister. As reported at page 3196 of Hansard I said this:
I wish to draw the minister's attention to the portion pertaining to the operation of motor vehicles. The minister will recall that when we were discussing Canadian National Railways in the special committee some time ago the president, Mr. Donald Gordon, made extensive reference to the operation of motor vehicles b.v the C.N.R. That is particularly important to me, because I wonder what significance this provision has with regard to the expansion of the services already in operation by the C.N.R. and the C.P.R.
The C.N.R. and the C.P.R. operate motor vehicles now, and I am wondering whether, if the C.N.R. gets permission through parliament to operate motor vehicles, the railway may be in a position of being able to override the provisions of any province regarding the issuance of licences for motor vehicles. I should like the minister to clear up this matter for me when he replies. As the situation stands today, if the railways want to operate motor vehicles in the city of Calgary, for example, they have to get a licence from the provincial government, and they must show need-
I want to emphasize that point. Under present conditions they must show need.
-before any more licences are issued so the industry will not be overcrowded, and in order to satisfy other precautions laid down by the province.
It was pointed out to us by Mr. Gordon, president of the C.N.R., that the railways were now using the operation of motor vehicles to extend, as he put it, competition with the trucking industry of Canada.
I made one slight further reference which I think I should put on the record. As reported on the next page I said this:
I am very much concerned about this matter, and I ask the minister to comment at some length on the statements I have made, particularly pertaining to the operation of motor vehicles by railway companies and the use of agreed charges.
I may say that I am not so greatly concerned at this moment about the matter of agreed charges, but I am definitely concerned about the invasion by the federal government of further provincial rights.
When the minister was speaking, I think he gave a forthright statement; and I think I so expressed myself when I was speaking on
[Mr. Johnston (Bow River) .1
that occasion. But I think the minister probably was deceived because when he, as he indicated this afternoon, took a second look at this bill, he found that it should have a few changes in order to make certain that some of the extensive powers which were being passed on to the Canadian National Railways were not carried out, in fact. But make no mistake about it, I do not think that Donald Gordon was deceived by it; not for a moment. Nor do I think that the solicitors who assisted in drawing up this legislation were deceived by it because they are too clever men to be deceived in that regard. I am not implying for a moment that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) is not just as clever, but, with all the duties he has, I can quite understand how his advisers even, or certainly Donald Gordon along with his advisers, could have slipped this over on him. That is very clearly brought out when the minister indicates that he has taken a second look at it and now proposes to bring in some amendments. Of course we do not know what they are, and as the Leader of the Opposition pointed out a while ago we must take only what is before us. We have the bill before us and we have all looked at it very carefully. We look upon it with some alarm. At page 3198 of Hansard of April 26 the minister answered me in this way:
At all events I should like to assure the members of the committee, and particularly the hon. member for Bow River, that there is no intention on the part of the government, in adding to the powers of the railway that of owning and operating motor vehicles, to make any sinister change of policy.
I am glad the minister said "sinister change" because that is exactly what is being done. Even though it may be unknown to the minister himself, it is a very sinister change of policy. The minister continued:
We merely intend to make a change which will enable the railways, in effect, to do through the parent company what they have been doing already through subsidiary companies.
I agree again with the Leader of the Opposition that last year when the Motor Vehicle Transport Act was passed the federal government made it very clear in the house and to the provinces that they did not want to interfere in any way with provincial rights as far as trucking is concerned and that even though they had the right to govern interprovincial trucking business they wanted to pass that right on to the provinces so there would be no confusion. Yet despite that assurance and despite the legislation that was passed they now come with a bill

which usurps every attempt to control trucking by the provincial governments. The minister went on to say:
There is no suggestion either that in granting this power the railway shall be free from the necessity of complying with the requirements of provincial governments so far as provincial laws apply to the operation of motor vehicles owned by the company.
I say again that I believe the Minister of Transport really believed that, but as he looks over the bill now I think he finds that he was in error in believing it. My reason for saying that is that the minister, having had a second look, has now said that he will have to bring in some amendments so that this power cannot be passed on to the railways. Of course, we do not know what the amendments are but we will find out. Then I went on to say:
May I ask the minister this question? Would that not be infringing on provincial rights? Could we legally put something like that in federal legislation, which would be a violation of provincial rights?
This happens to be the section that the Leader of the Opposition quoted but I think I should put it on the record again for the sake of continuity. The minister said:
I do not think it would be an infringement, Mr. Chairman. I believe it is competent for parliament to empower a federal corporation to operate motor vehicles. I do not believe, for instance, that merely because the power is derived from parliament the operator of the motor vehicles could claim he would not be subject to the laws of the province in the operation of those motor vehicles.
May I point out to the minister that if the bill is passed in its present form that is exactly what the railway companies would be able to do. They would have overriding rights over any provincial legislation. The minister continued: .
I think my hon. friend could find many examples of dominion corporations operating motor vehicles strictly in conformity with provincial requirements.
I am pointing this out, Mr. Speaker, because I want the house to understand thoroughly the position which I took on that occasion. I was fearful of this very thing and I tried to indicate it to the minister so that he would be on the alert for anything of this nature. I am not going to say it was because I spoke on that occasion that the minister took a second look at the legislation, but nevertheless he did so and as a result he has now indicated he intends to bring in certain amendments. On that occasion I had this to say:
May I ask the minister this? Suppose the province decided that it was not necessary to have another trucking concern within the province or within the city where the company was making its application. Suppose the province said they would refuse to grant a licence on the ground that the operation was not necessary. Would they be
Canadian National Railways
able to do that if we granted the company parliamentary authority to carry on this type of operation?
The minister answered:
There are some constitutional aspects of that question which I would hesitate to try to dispose of summarily. I suppose the question would come up as to whether it was an integral part of the railway operation. All I can say to my hon. friend, and I hope he will be satisfied with it, is that there is no intention in the legislation to relieve the railways of the necessity of complying with the requirements of the province in the operation of these motor vehicles.
There again I think the minister intimated very clearly that, so far as he was concerned, he did not think that power was in the bill but, Mr. Speaker, I can assure you I think it is there.

Mr. Speaker, when we called it six o'clock I was speaking in the debate on second reading of Bill 351, and I had pointed out that there were things which had crept into the writing of the bill which, in my opinion, were not then known to the Minister of Transport, and that when he gave his statement to the house the other day saying, in effect, that it was not the intention of the government to extend the powers of the railways over truck transport any more than it then possessed, he made that statement in all sincerity. I believe he did, but that he had one put over on him when those who framed the legislation drew it up. I think the minister would almost agree with my statement in that particular.
I should like now to go a little further with what I was saying before six o'clock, when I was pointing out the minister had indicated that there are one or two places in the proposed bill where he intends to have some changes made. He did indicate that where part III of the first schedule refers to the Canadian National Transportation, Limited-

Canadian National Railways it changed so that it will make sure that there is not any misunderstanding with regard to the powers being allotted to the railway companies.

Yes, to which part III applies. Well, that is a very broad statement, because I do not know to just what other parts part III of the first schedule applies. So again I must take what is in the bill.
I am afraid however that there are other parts of the first schedule that would appear somewhat suspicious-that is, parts other than the one to which the minister referred. For instance, there are several references in the first schedule to the Canadian National Express Company. Now, the Canadian National Express Company operates trucks. To what extent they could go ahead and operate trucks to accomplish the same purpose, I do not know.
Then, reference is made to the Canadian National Transfer Company.
Clause 27 in the bill gives the railways extreme powers, when it authorizes them to operate motor vehicles of all kinds and to lease them. It gives power to-
-maintain and operate motor vehicles on highways in Canada or elsewhere for the carriage of traffic and may charge tolls therefor.
Unless that section were done away with, too, it seems to me that, regardless of whether the minister changes something in the first schedule, the railways would still have the power to enter a province and start a trucking business. As I said the other day, they could operate a truck line between Calgary and Edmonton, regardless of the protests of the province-and this, even though the schedule was changed.
Clause 27 is indeed a most dangerous one for the provinces, because the railways could go in and override any provincial legislation contemplated by the provinces, or legislation then in existence.
Then, too, there is contemplated in clause 18 of the bill a most dangerous provision. I would draw the minister's attention to the very first line of that clause where it says: "The railway or other transportation works". In that section, regardless of whether or not the minister removes some of the items in the first schedule, that line in clause 18 which refers to "the railway or other transportation works" could include, in my judgment, any
TMr. Johnston (Bow River).]

type of truck transport the railways might want to operate. And unless it was indicated specifically that "the railway or other transportation works" excluded those referred to in clause 27, then the railways would be able to operate in any way they saw fit. But if it was indicated in clause 18 that the "transportation works" excluded those referred to in clause 27, the section so amended might have some bearing on that matter. Then in the second part of clause 18 it refers to "the works of every company that is comprised in Canadian National Railways". There, too, is a tremendous leeway for the company.
So again I draw to the minister's attention the fact that, even though he were to remove part of the first schedule-which he says he is going to do-I do not think this action alone would be sufficient, because there are other places in the proposed bill that would give the railways the right to carry on operations as fully as they intend to. Because certainly the term "Canadian National Railways" is used on many occasions, and it seems to me that term is broad enough to allow the railways to operate trucks in any manner they see fit.
I say again that I do not think for one moment this was an oversight by the railway company, because they are too shrewd, by far, to allow a thing like this to escape their attention, particularly when on almost every occasion they have made particular efforts to squeeze the trucking business out of existence-not merely to put it on a fair, reasonable and competitive basis, not at all, but to squeeze it right out of existence so that they can monopolize the whole transportation system.
Oh, if we wanted to go into agreed charges -that, too, is another matter. But, mind you, they would hardly need agreed charges if this bill went through as now framed. They would have no competition from the trucks. Mr. Gordon said in committee, in effect, he was not going to give trucks any advantage. He could get rid of them. And, make no mistake about it, that is what they have in mind.

speechtext:
Your Honour will realize that I referred to the clause because the hon. member for Fort William had made specific reference to it. And that is another point to which I would draw the minister's attention. There is an important background in this of which I think we should take cognizance. The reason I am so concerned is that the bill proposes to insert the words-and the Minister of Transport has already made reference to this, so I suggest I am not out of order in repeating these words-
The works of every company that is comprised in Canadian National Railways but is not incorporated by or under the laws of Canada are hereby declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada.
That appears in two places in the clause- "for the general advantage of Canada"-and indicates the damage which could result from any bill using those words, particularly this bill.
To give some idea of the importance of that clause in the bill I wish to refer to another article from a prominent individual in Canada who is now dead. I draw to your attention again, sir, that those who put that expression in the bill knew without doubt what they were doing. I refer to the particular words that I mentioned a moment ago "for the general advantage of Canada." To give you some idea of the tremendous importance of this section, I want to quote from an outstanding authority on legal matters, the former chief justice of Canada, the late Right Hon. Sir Lyman Poore Duff, when he commented in the course of replying to certain questions referred to the Supreme Court of Canada by the governor general in council in October, 1929, as follows:
The authority created by section 92 (10) (c) is of a most unusual nature. It is an authority given
Canadian National Railways
to the dominion parliament to clothe itself with jurisdiction-exclusive jurisdiction-in respect of subjects over which, in the absence of such action by parliament, exclusive control is, and would remain vested in the provinces. Parliament is empowered to withdraw from that control matters coming within such subjects, and to assume jurisdiction itself. It wields an authority which enables it, in effect, to rearrange the distribution of legislative powers effected directly by the act, and, in some views of the enactment, to bring about changes of the most radical import, in that distribution:-
This is one example in the bill. I continue: -and the basis and condition of its action must be the decision by parliament that the "work or undertaking" or class of works or undertakings affected by that action is "for the general advantage of Canada", or of two or more of the provinces: which decision must be evidenced and authenticated by a solemn declaration, in that sense, by parliament itself.
That has reference to the British North America Act, Mr. Speaker. When the framers of this legislation put the section under discussion in the bill they knew that when this transport bill was given this wide power and Canadian National Transportation, Limited, was included in that, along with similar expressions, they were taking away from the provinces every vestige of control over trucking within their boundaries.
The British North America Act has this to say about the expression "for the general advantage of Canada". Section 92 of the British North America Act reads:
Exclusive Powers of Provincial Legislatures.
92. In each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated; that is to say,-
Subsection 10 (c) enumerates them and reads:
Such works as, although wholly situate within the province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces.
By placing these words in the bill, the railways are permitted to enter any province, even though that province has enjoyed the exclusive rights over transportation and trucking for 100 years, and usurp the whole powers of the province.

speechtext: They always have since confederation.

subsubtopic: AUTHORIZA- TION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext:
Even though they have exercised such powers, there is no reason why we should delegate that by statute, and it would be a very bad mistake, Mr. Speaker, to do it.
The late Sir Lyman Duff recognized the importance of that section in the British North America Act, and he pointed out that wherever the federal legislation has drawn

Canadian National Railways on it and has used that expression, it has been used for the express purpose of taking absolute control of those subjects over which provincial governments have always exercised their jurisdiction. We must be very careful in this house that we do not exercise any more powers of centralization than we already have.
I suggest to the minister that when he brings in his amendments to the bill, which he says he intends to do, he should not overlook changing clause 18 and clause 27 and all those other parts of the bill which refer to motor transportation. I hope he will see that these clauses are withdrawn from the bill and that there are no further infringements upon provincial rights.
There is just one more word that I should like to say in regard to this matter. When the bill is referred to the committee, I hope the minister will make the order of reference sufficiently wide so that all parties concerned in this matter, the trucking organizations, the railways and others, will have the right to come before the committee and state their case and have this legislation drawn up in the interests of all of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall trespass on the time of the house for only a moment. There are one or two provisions of this bill which I must take exception to. This afternoon the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) objected to this legislation on the ground that the trucking provision was a violation, or an invasion, of provincial rights. Frankly, I cannot get too excited about that aspect of the act, although I am sure my colleagues, the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin) and the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon), will comment on it. I oppose this bill for another reason.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the main purpose of the Canadian National Railways should be to run a railway. It seems to me also, that the main purpose of the executive and the officials of that company, should be to concentrate all of their efforts on running that railway, in a successful way.
Any hon. member who looks at the C.N.R. balance sheet, even in a superficial way, knows that so far the present management has not been able to make a financial success of our government-owned railway. Three years ago Mr. Donald Gordon and the government came to this parliament, and asked for a reorganization of the capital structure of the Canadian National Railways. The net effect of that reorganization was to wipe out more than $1 billion and substitute therefor
(Mr. Johnston (Bow River).]
non-interest bearing stocks. The government told us at that time that, if the reorganization was proceeded with, future balance sheets of the Canadian National Railways should be a good deal better; the profit and loss statement should improve. To a degree perhaps it has, but the over-all picture is still pretty bad as far as the Canadian taxpayer is concerned. But this year once again the Canadian National Railways have shown a huge deficit of $28-7 million.
All Canadians realize the role which the Canadian National Railways have played and are playing in the opening up and in the developing of the Dominion of Canada. Most of our citizens are willing to finance capital expenditures for the Canadian National Railways when they are used for that purpose- namely the opening up of the Dominion of Canada. But in my opinion they are neither willing nor anxious to pay taxes to permit the Canadian National Railways to embark on a lot of side enterprises apart from railroading merely to duplicate or compete with existing facilities. Such a trend is becoming more prevalent every year within the Canadian National Railways.
Last year, despite the fact that the railroad was operating at a substantial loss, the government came to us and demanded the fantastic sum of $20 million to build a luxury hotel in the city of Montreal. They asked for that huge sum, despite the fact that there were already dozens of other hotels in Montreal, and despite the fact that the existing Canadian National hotels, for the most part, had over a period of years not been profitable.
The bill that is before us tonight permits the Canadian National Railways to go into a good many business enterprises other than railroads. For instance, one clause of this bill permits the company to construct or acquire telecommunication facilities in Canada or elsewhere in the world. I ask hon. members to note the word "elsewhere". What is the government policy in regard to telecommunications? What new investment is proposed? What extension is planned elsewhere in the world? Precisely how will this extension help the Canadian taxpayer? I think the minister should answer those questions.
This afternoon the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) assured parliament that, as far as trucking was concerned, this bill proposed no great change in government policy. I think he made that statement to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew). I hope the minister will pardon me if I say that it is a little difficult for hon. members to accept his words at face value. Because what is

the minister saying? He is saying in effect: "We want these new powers which will permit the C.N.R. to go into trucking, but we are not going to use them". Why ask for powers which will not be used? I just do not see the logic of such a position.
As I read clause 27, the C.N.R. would be given wide and comprehensive powers which would permit them if they so desired to go into both the trucking and bus businesses. Such a development would inevitably mean a substantial investment by the taxpayers of Canada. Surely, before this bill passes, the minister should tell parliament what investment the C.N.R. proposes to make in trucking, and precisely why this step is necessary.
I cannot convince myself that the C.N.R. should go into the trucking business at this time. I think such a step would be undesirable; I think it would be unfortunate; and I think it would be contrary to sound business principles. What is more important, I do not think it would be in the interests of the Canadian taxpayer.
Clause 29 of the bill is even more revealing.

speechtext:
This is a bill to permit the C.N.R. to go into the trucking and bus business. But in addition it may go into such businesses as wharves, docks, dockyards, slips, elevators, offices, warehouses and other buildings. Just where is this going to end? If the C.N.R. were going to finance all these side enterprises out of profits I probably would not have much objection, but such is not the case. Today the C.N.R. has invested substantial sums of money in sidelines other than the railways, and it is taking the money for such unnecessary expansions directly from the pockets of the Canadian taxpayer. Before hon. members agree to the passage of this bill they should realize that every single Canadian is going to have to dig down into his pockets to help finance the expansions which Mr. Gordon and the government are planning.
It seems to me that Mr. Gordon and the C.N.R. officials first of all should make a financial success of running their railroad. Then when they have done that, if they so desire they can come to parliament to ask for additional money to run these sidelines.
I was disappointed this afternoon when neither the Leader of the Opposition nor the
Canadian National Railways hon. member for Bow River moved an amendment to this bill. It seems to me that the matter is too important to rush through, so I am going to move an amendment. I may have trouble finding five hon. members to stand up, but I shall worry about that when the time comes. I wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon):
That Bill No. 351 be not now read a second time, but that it be read this day six months.
This afternoon the Leader of the Opposition expressed the belief that a conference should be called with the provinces before this matter was settled. If he believes that, and I am sure he does, I hope that he will find it possible to support this amendment, which would make it possible for his wishes to be carried out.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill No. 351 now before the house, and entitled "an act respecting Canadian National Railways", cannot be of small concern to those who uphold and favour private enterprise in Canada. Nor can it fail to retain the attention of true Canadians, particularly the staunch defenders of provincial autonomy, as guaranteed by the British North America Act.
We note that the main purpose of the bill is to enable the Canadian railways to operate a highway transport system in any of the Canadian provinces and even from one province to another.
According to the bill, the Canadian National would be entitled to operate a trucking business for the transport of goods as well as a bus service for the transport of passengers.
Mr. Speaker, more and more the government is launching out into a dangerous socialist policy conducive to nationalization of the transport system, whether by rail or motor vehicle.
Little by little a nefarious centralization policy is being developed, which, on the one hand, will gradually destroy private enterprise and, on the other hand, deprive provincial authorities of powers which belong to them de jure and; de facto.
To allow the Canadian National to operate such a transportation system would be a serious breach of the principles recognized since confederation and would amount to a systematic and gradual scuttling of private enterprise.
The contents of this bill show that the government intends to practise unfair and unjust competition with regard to people who

Canadian National Railways invested considerable capital, or small savings, in transport companies for the conveyance of goods or in bus companies for the transport of passengers. Should this bill be passed, it would be a serious encroachment upon the most elementary definition of democracy, because it would also cause a slow but painful and sure death to the transport industry in Canada.
I cannot bring myself to believe that the idea behind this bill originated in the mind of the Minister of Transport, for whom I have the greatest regard. I do fear, however, that it may be the irresponsible work of some powerful bureaucrat whose influence within the Canadian National Railways and the Department of Transport overshadows the influence that should be exercised first and foremost by the minister.
It is inconceivable that such a bill should have been introduced without due regard for its disastrous consequences, not only for the existing transportation industry but also for all Canadian taxpayers. It must be remembered that the proposed new subsidiaries connected with the Canadian National Railways, and whose establishment parliament is being asked to ratify by this bill, will be set up with the money and to the prejudice of the people.
All existing private companies already give full and complete satisfaction to their customers, whether it be for the transport of passengers or freight.
Those companies, large and small, were generally established as a result of enormous sacrifices made in the best interests of the patrons as well as in that of the operators. The competition they will now have to face will be considerable and it is to be feared that most of them will eventually fold up or face bankruptcy. Private enterprise is certainly in no position to face government competition, a competition which can, at any time, drive out private competition because of the vastly larger capital at its command. It must not be forgotten that it may call upon the people's money as it wishes.
Should the Canadian National Railways one day take a fancy to remain alone in the transport business in this country and to eliminate all their competitors, they could achieve their purpose with the greatest of ease. Might, in this case, would make right.
Not being subject to the laws in force in the various provinces of this country and being subjected to no authority but that of the
[Mr. Dufresne.l
board of transport commissioners, which comes under federal jurisdiction, the Canadian National Railways can, at any time, wage a price war upon those which stand in their way. On the railways' recommendation alone the board could approve of a reduction in rates in any of the provinces of this country, with no regard for possible consequences.
Why should the Canadian National worry about profit and losses in its operations, since this is a government owned business? If, at year's end, it finds itself facing a deficit, it can always call upon the Canadian government to use its majority in this house to vote such amounts as are necessary to make good the deficit. One fact which will be forgotten then, as it so often was in the past, is that in this case, as in others, it is the Canadian taxpayer who always foots the bill.
This measure, Mr. Speaker, sets a very dangerous precedent and jeopardizes the future of private enterprise. It brings us a step closer to a reprehensible centralization, which wide-awake people are trying to check. What is worse, some sections of that bill are nothing less than a direct provocation to the provincial authorities, which, up to now, had control over the transport industry in Canada.
The section of the bill which prevents provincial authorities from exercising their jurisdiction over the operation of various Canadian National services making use of the provincial highways, which were built with moneys collected in the respective provinces, is an invitation to disorder. It is not the first time, by the way, that the Liberal government of Ottawa sets such a bad example.
Even if it were only for the reason I just mentioned, I hope that the Minister of Transport will agree to withdraw the bill now before the house, for the protection first of private enterprise in Canada and then of the poor taxpayer who cannot foresee in the future that relief so urgently needed.
Mr. Speaker, since this discussion has been mainly on two sections of the bill to which a majority of members seem opposed, I wonder if the Minister of Transport could not split up this bill into two parts? Why not bring down a bill to consolidate the existing legislation which is enacted again in this Bill 351, and then bring down a special bill on the question which concerns most members as well as the provinces and all those who hold a position in our private transport industry?

In other words, ducking the issue. As far as I am concerned, one of the crying needs in this country today is for a national transportation system. When you take a look at the freight rates across this country, with the development of transportation in the air carrying both passengers and cargo, the St. Lawrence seaway which will provide another means of transportation fairly well across the country and the trucking business that is being built up straight across Canada, if we are sensible I think we must realize that some time someone must have the courage to take hold of the whole transportation system across the country, bring it under one regulatory body somewhere and see if he cannot get some sanity into the whole system, with the possibility of the equalization of freight rates, whether the transportation is by air, land or water, by means of trucking or by railroads. I think that procedure is a "must" and that it will have to come. I think this bill is a step in that direction. First, it is an attempt to bring under one set of covers all of the statutes that have to do with the Canadian National Railways so that it will be a handy reference for anyone who wants to talk about railway legislation.
As far as the C.N.R. is concerned, may I say that I have served year by year on the committee that looks after their accounts. I have served on that committee fairly continuously since coming to the house. While the railway is doing many things that we do not like, nevertheless we must recognize this fact. This railway is serving many sections of this country that otherwise would

Canadian National Railways not be getting any service at all; if it is to be on a straight commercial basis, there would be no service. If you are going to measure the service of the railway and its value to the country in terms of dollars and cents, then you will tear up a great deal of the mileage of the Canadian National Railways.
When someone says that in this house a couple of years ago we wrote off a huge debt for the Canadian National Railways, may I point out that we did no such thing. We relieved the Canadian National Railways of a debt which they inherited, not one which they built up. The Canadian National Railways took over many operating railroads in this country when they were in bankruptcy or when they should have been put into bankruptcy. But instead of doing that, the C.N.R. took over those companies and also their bonds and continued to pay these bonds and the interest on them year by year, a procedure which piled up a huge deficit charged to the Canadian National Railways but which should have been written off in a bankruptcy court many years previously. Most of the members who have been here for some time and who have taken an interest in the struggles of the C.N.R. realize that the writing off of that debt was something that was proper. But do not think it was charity to the C.N.R. It was no such thing.
In the second place, unless the truckers, the airways and others are prepared to sit down and to come under one set of legislation, with someone in authority to regulate the future of transportation in the country, the situation is going to get worse and worse all the time. At least this is an attempt to get gathered together all of the legislation pertaining to that particular system so that you may have a handy reference and see exactly where the pieces of legislation fit in. If we want to measure the C.N.R. in terms of dollars and cents or profits, then we shall be obliged to discontinue a great deal of service across this country. I know that no member of this house is prepared to do that. In my judgment, the expansion in other fields is merely an attempt to get money in order to continue the service that is necessary. Unless they get that money, the C.N.R. are not going to be able to serve many of the unprofitable sections they are serving today.
I am prepared to make a decision on this bill now. There are many sideline issues that we can argue with Mr. Gordon. We do argue them with him and we shall continue to do so. However, I do not think they should be confused with this particular bill. I see nothing wrong with the bill. I think it

is a step in the right direction. I think that we are going to have to go further than this. I think we are going to have to have transport under some regulatory body in order that we may get some sanity into freight rates on transportation by sea, land and air. This is something that must come, and it is not too far away. As far as I am concerned, I am prepared to support this bill now and to take a look at it in the future to see whether it is working out properly or otherwise.

This topic was fairly well discussed this afternoon. Second, as I understand it, the C.N.R. was formed with the knowledge that the Canadian taxpayers were taking over a pretty poor business risk. We had businesses that were bankrupt and the Canadian government stepped in for purposes best known to itself at that time. Each of us can read the history of what happened, but apparently it was considered essential to keep our northland open in an economic way. My third reason is that we are apparently going to try to put out of business now the truckers who are actually subsidizing this very railway at this time. In other words, it is being done in the same way as my C.C.F. friends do in my own riding when they get the I.W.A. to support them and the Social Credit members of that organization also have to contribute 50 cents apiece to help to put me out of office. They have no alternative because the majority rules. The same thing applies here so far as the truckers are concerned.
To deal with each of these points in its own perspective, let me refer first to the question of the infringement of provincial rights. This evening the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) mentioned that the late Chief Justice Lyman Duff had brought to our attention the necessity of exercising caution in respect of the infringement of provincial rights. I believe he did that in 1929 when dealing with a water act. Then earlier than that there was the case of Luscar Collieries Ltd. v. N. S. McDonald which is to be found in 1925 and 1927 Canada Supreme Court Reports. It was a very similar case and the justices of the day found reasons for bringing a spur line of
Canadian National Railways some 51 or 5| miles under the jurisdiction of the C.N.R. They did so not by reason of the fact that it was in the interests of Canada under section 92 (10) (c) of the British North America Act-they scrapped that idea altogether-but rather by reason of the fact that they decided it was in the interests of Canadian National Railways, the spur was an integral part of the railway and must be treated as such. My second reason for opposing the bill is that when the C.N.R. was formed it was done with the full knowledge that the Canadian taxpayers were taking over a poor business risk. The people of Canada realized at that time that there were many bankrupt railways involved by reason of the fact that unnecessary risks were taken by venture capital to open up various regions of Canada with the hope that Canada would grow by such leaps and bounds that everybody would be wealthy who owned shares in these railways. I draw to the attention of my C.C.F. friends again that private enterprise capital is quite ready to risk money when it thinks it has an even chance of succeeding, and that was the case at that time. Unfortunately the country was not ready to be opened up as quickly as these people had hoped with the result that Canadian National Railways was formed to take over many of these bankrupt or practically bankrupt companies.
In taking over these railways we discovered they were not and could not be profitable because they were not constructed along profitable routes. There was not sufficient industry or a large enough number of people along the lines to make and keep these railways profitable. So the railway business began to go into other fields, and that is the danger I see in the bill now before us. Last year we voted an expenditure of some $20 million to enable the railway to go further into the hotel business. Mr. Speaker, because the bill now before the house entails encroachments upon the rights of the
Canadian National Railways provinces, it is fitting that strong protest be voiced against those encroachments and I shall do so now although very briefly.
If the bill is passed in its present form, operations of the Canadian National bus and truck companies would come under the jurisdiction of the federal board of transport commissioners. It is an ill-chosen time to encroach upon provincial autonomy.
The Canadian National has no right to be placed in a privileged position toward its competitors. It should be subject to the same regulations and enjoy the same privileges as other similar organizations.
If there is one firm on which provincial authorities should keep an eye and whose operations should be supervised by those it serves most directly, it is the Canadian National.
As everyone knows, and I have said so many times, the province of Quebec is not getting from the Canadian National Railways the treatment to which it is entitled in all fairness. More often than not, the company's management has turned a deaf ear to our claims and requests.
As far as my particular district is concerned, the minister knows that the railway line from Montreal to Chicoutimi has long ceased to meet the needs of our population.
Twelve hours to cover 300 miles is far too long for the pleasure one gets on such trains where, most of the time, there is no dining car.
Stations along this line leave much to be desired in the way of comfort. The Canadian National Railways service in our part of the country is that of an old railway line built almost 70 years ago to serve the few villages of settlers then established in the Lake St. John district.
Today, with its grade crossings, its old station and its dilapidated buildings, it mars the city of Chicoutimi.
We have always had trouble getting some necessary improvements and our efforts were not more fruitful when we asked for the St. Felicien-Chibougamau railway.
I should hope that the Minister of Transport will soon be in a position to give us some better news on this matter. I have no intention of reverting now to this subject.
I merely wish to record my opposition to this bill because it contains clauses which encroach upon provincial rights and also because it carries us a step further along the road to the artificial paradise of the socialists and their state paternalism.

Canadian National Railways
The Canadian National Railways are not as yet able to operate at a profit. They are a sick business, as was recently stated by Mr. Fairweather, vice-president for research.
Their ailments and failings will not be remedied by giving them power to enter into the truck and bus business.
Their management will only find there a further opportunity for piling deficit upon deficit. Mind you, I do not think they lack the required ability, but I am convinced that they have to feed a white elephant which had to be taken off the hands of those who had brought it forth to save them from bankruptcy.
The Canadian National Railways are putting up a new hotel in Montreal. It should, by the way, be called Chateau Maisonneuve. A recent article in Maclean's magazine showed how logical it would be to give it that name, which has been recommended by the people of my province. This establishment will be rented to American capitalists. Will the same thing be done with the bus and truck lines which it is proposed to organize under the terms of this legislation? If these services are profitable, why not keep the profit? If not, why set them up?
The Canadian National is already enough of a drain on the taxpayers' pocketbook. It should not be given the means to be a further charge upon them. I therefore second the motion introduced by our colleague, the member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher). I do so because I am against centralization in any way, shape or form, and against socialism, even when it is advocated by the hon. gentlemen opposite.
