Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to waste the time of the house in useless repetitions; nevertheless I wish to voice my opposition to the passage of Bill No. 351 and explain why I shall vote in favour of the amendment.
While I do not have the advantage of being a lawyer, I shall risk an opinion in a field where I can very possibly err.
In my humble opinion, if the bill is adopted without amendment, it will remove from the jurisdiction of the provinces the various bus and truck lines and connected highway transport services operated by the Canadian National Railways.
While I know it is against the rules to discuss in detail the particular section which will .create that situation, I can well say that

this will be one of the general results-and not the least-of the adoption of the bill.
I stand to be corrected if I am wrong but I think that, even if in this case we do not infringe upon the letter of the constitution, we are surely going against its spirit.
It is quite easy to foresee, without too great a stretch of the imagination, the development and the importance that might be taken on some day by what the bill calls, in questionable French, "les ouvrages de chemins de fer ou autre ouvrage de transport". This means the possible development of fleets of trucks for the transport of goods, and of bus lines with many powerful units for the transport of passengers. And all that outside the jurisdiction of our provincial legislatures, which are nevertheless responsible for transport and traffic legislation within their boundaries, as well as for the onerous job of building and maintaining a highway system which is extremely costly for our provincial and municipal administrations.
Anyone conscious of the sometimes unbounded ambitions of the Canadian National Railways officials can well wonder whether the new transport organizations authorized under this bill will not some day become more important than all those which at the present time come under private enterprise.
We would then be faced with a strange and abnormal situation where provincial jurisdiction in a most important field of its own would be practically inefficient and inoperative, since it could not operate in a very important part of its sphere, which would then be under the jurisdiction of another political body.
But, even if this bill did not threaten to facilitate the gaining of a foothold in the field of provincial autonomy, the fact remains that it would represent a socialist measure which should be rejected, because it does not correspond to a real need and would in no way remedy the few abuses or inconveniences that may result from or be maintained by the present system.
On the contrary, this legislation would involve unfair competition with private enterprise, which has made considerable sacrifices in order to set up a suitable system, and would make the taxpayers responsible for the liabilities of a competitor who frequently shows a deficit, which he passes on to the taxpayer, instead of paying for his errors himself.

I would, moreover, Mr. Speaker, point out another fact which is familiar to me: there are a great number of small communities and remote and sparsely populated localities, where the larger transport organizations are not interested in operating, because there is no profit in it. These limited territories are served by individuals who are able, owing to their work, their efforts and their sense of economy to operate with a small margin of profit which allows them all the same to earn their living and, at the same time, be of help to the communities they serve.
It is to be feared, Mr. Speaker, that any future transport organizations of the Canadian National Railways of Canada will enter these territories and operate at a loss while competing unfairly with pioneers who have had and still have the merit of being selfsupporting and do not ask their patrons to pay for their occasional losses. If, in these nice spring days, the Canadian National Railways suddenly feel the fever of expansion, they could, instead of embarking upon new ventures which will probably result in new deficits, try to calm this fever by undertaking urgent works which are actually and exclusively within their field, such as the construction of the railway line connecting Chibougamau and St. Felicien.

I wonder how we would feel if constantly, day after day, there was someone who had some new axe to grind in connection with the company that might employ us? Therefore, I say, by all means let us make this a business type operation. Let us give it the opportunity to be run as a good business. I do not think we will have accomplished that unless we are prepared to accept the ordinary principles of company organization and operation in the direction of this great public enterprise, the same principles used in connection with the direction and operation of our largest private corporations.
If we ask the people to look at the company in that light then I think it is clear that we should expect those who direct the enterprise to look on their duties in the same way. We should expect adequate direction from the head people of this corporation and we should expect them to appear before the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines once a year ready to make a complete disclosure of the operations of the company. If it so happens that we are not satisfied with their stewardship during the previous year obviously there is only one answer-they need replacing. But they should not be harassed from day to day into the ensuing year.
When I look at this act I wonder if one of the failings in connection with the direction of the company can be found in certain observations by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) who indicated in the house that he was loath to see a type of arbitrary control concentrated in one man. As a matter of fact I think the president of the Canadian National Railways would welcome the additional advice and help which he would get from a larger board of directors.
It is unheard of that a company of this size should be operating with a board of directors of seven and directed with an executive quorum of only four. The board of directors should be representative of the best business minds in the country. I am sure that there is no dearth of material and I am sure that there would be no reluctance on the part of anyone if the government should see fit to increase the membership on the board of directors, even to fifteen. Let us have the advice of the best businessmen we can get and avoid any indication that we are running a one-man show.
I think in the company there is unswerving loyalty to the president, but I think also that

Canadian National Railways the employees ask if it is not possible that within the ranks of that great organization there are men of a calibre who could head the enterprise which they may have served in for most of their adult years. For the maintenance of employee morale I think it will be necessary in the future to indicate to these employees that there is no job not open to them, not even at the top.
I think also that there is a necessity for better public relations. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) referred to the obligations which had been handed down and placed upon this railway. It is time that we told the public the true story of that burden and indicated in its true relationship the job which the company is doing and can do.
I come now to the question of stewardship. It seems to me that we must attempt if it is at all possible to get this company, this management, on all fours with the provisions of the Companies Act. I like to think that everyone in this country is a shareholder in this railway and that once a year the members of the standing committee hold voting proxies for those people. Once a year the management should come to them and make a complete disclosure of the operations of the past year. It may be that we are not entitled to information in advance which may affect company policy, but I am quite sure that at the end of the year at the time when ordinarily shareholders would pass a resolution confirming the acts of the directors for the previous year a full disclosure should be made to that committee. In regard to reports and opinions when dealing with companies I should like to read from Masten and Fraser's "Company Law of Canada", page 658:
As regards the right of inspecting reports and opinions, the principle is that, shareholders having a common interest in the company's property, an opinion having regard to such property paid for out of the company's earnings is the common property of the shareholders; but the principle does not apply where the interests of the company and the shareholders are adverse and the parties are sundered by litigation: Woodhouse & Co. Limited v. Woodhouse (1914) 30 T.L.R.559.
Then I think of the employees of this company as being shareholders, and I quote from the same publication at page 720:
A by-law or resolution of the directors will be invalid and ultra vires of the company if it operates unequally towards the interests of any class of the shareholders: North-west Electric Co. v. Walsh (1899) 29 S.C.R.33.
I think of these employee-shareholders as being a special type of shareholders and I wonder when such agreements are entered into as the one with the Hilton corporation if we are not passing bylaws or resolutions

which are ultra vires of the company because they react unequally towards the interests of a class of shareholders. When we do that we foreclose those people from an opportunity to get to the top in their chosen profession.
Then in connection with borrowing money and the provision of the Companies Act in connection therewith, in the case of an ordinary company it is necessary for two-thirds of the shareholders to confirm a borrowing bylaw. This is protection for the shareholders of the company, so that there will not be any steamrollering which may affect the physical assets or the securities of the corporation unless two-thirds of the shareholders approve. Yet in the operation of this company over the last year we have seen a tendency to steamroller special provisions in connection with borrowing money in connection with which we have not been given adequate information.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that I am not supposed to refer to specific sections in connection with this legislation, but I do not believe I can pass without saying this. Unless there is some general provision in connection with the holding of these directorships, it is possible for even Conrad Hilton himself to be appointed to this board. I see nothing in here which restricts the appointment of the chairman of the board to a person who is a Canadian citizen.
In addition I note something unusual as well, that the president of this company may not be a director-a very unusual type of arrangement, as you find that in the Companies Act it is necessary that the president of the company be on the board of directors. I wonder what type of operation we can expect, unless the man who is closest to the administrative functions of the company is sitting around the table with the rest of the directors. These are provisions which must be studied closely.
There are aspects we have talked about today in connection with federal and provincial jurisdictions, but to make this company work and work well there are the problems of personnel and their morale. Let us see that between meetings of the standing committee this company is allowed to plot its own course and do its own job. Let us free it from the everyday sniping, but then once a year bring it strictly to account before the shareholders and make full disclosure of all the facts that should be presented at any annual shareholders' meeting.

Mr. Speaker, there are very few occasions when I have the pleasure of thanking a member of the opposition for services rendered. This time I want to express my appreciation

to the hon. member for York West (Mr. Hamilton) for having confirmed in every way what I said the other day about the powers of the chairman of the Canadian National Railways. In that respect I have some excerpts, one from a deeply Conservative paper, the Ottawa Journal, and another from the Toriest of all Tory papers, the Post-Record, of Sydney, which I shall read. The other day I said that it was the Tory policy to prevent members of parliament from inquiring about what is being done. I do not wish to disturb my hon. friend. I shall try to be as gracious to him as he has been gracious to me, but I want him to know the truth about the management of the Canadian National Railways and its dealings with the parliament of Canada.
There are two policies. There is the Liberal policy and there is the Conservative policy. The Liberal policy is to the effect that members of parliament have an unquestionable right to secure information from the management of the railway and to exercise the necessary control over the expenditures. That is the Liberal policy.

subsubtopic: AUTHORIZA- TION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext: Why don't they follow it?

subsubtopic: AUTHORIZA- TION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext:
This is why the committee is called, to hear the statements of Mr. Gordon and his staff. Then there is the Conservative policy, which is to the effect that the Canadian National Railways shall be left alone to manage the company in a true business manner without any interference from politicians like my hon. friend from York West, the member for Temiscouata, and all of those. It is the kind of policy of laissez faire which has been so well described by Thackeray in his essays, which my hon. friend must remember better than I do, as he is younger than I am and his reading of that must be fresher in his memory. The Tory policy is a policy of laissez faire. Let well enough alone; do not intervene in the good management of the Canadian National Railways; leave them alone; they are experts and they know what they have to do. We politicians must bow to them. We must let them do all they want, always provided that it is not done by the politicians, and provided that the politicians do not interfere with the management.
My hon. friend from York West suggested that the number of directors should be increased. Why? No one is consulted. Why should we have more? At the present time there are six or seven, and Mr. Gordon pays no attention to them, just as if they did not exist. My hon. friend suggests that they should be more numerous. Why not consult the members of parliament? We have the committee. As a classical example, I asked 50433-255i
Canadian National Railways Mr. Gordon to tell me the price that he had paid for fence posts-something like that, but bigger. My hon. friend would be surprised. Mr. Gordon has very much confidence-and I am very glad that Mr. Gordon was not a professor of philosophy. He told me that it was unethical to inquire about the price paid for fence posts by the Canadian National Railways. We do not have the same ethics.

subsubtopic: AUTHORIZA- TION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext: They were not political fence posts?

subsubtopic: AUTHORIZA- TION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext: No, they were supposed to be made of good timber-cedar fences. Then my hon. friend was a learned barrister at law and he had the law in hand when he told us that the decisions of the company must be confirmed by two-thirds of the shareholders. He had a big book and he quoted precedents, just the same as he would have done before parliament sitting as a high court-the high court of the land. My hon. friend knows one thing and many more; but there is one thing that he does not know or that he has forgotten. It is that the companies incorporated by virtue of the Companies Act of Canada or the companies act of any province are supposed to make regulations to govern their meetings. Although my hon. friend has not been sitting here long he is too experienced a member to ignore the laws of the land and he is too conversant with them to do so. It is too bad that, instead of wasting his time in reading a big book on company law, he has not read the previous reports of the railways and shipping committee which contain extremely interesting material.

Yes.
I will ask my friend the hon. member for York West to listen to this. I am not speaking. It is Mr. Gordon who is speaking.

speechtext:
There is no such thing, Mr. Pouliot. What happens is this, the board of directors meets on a date which is agreed, and in practice we meet once a month. During the course of the board of directors' meetings, questions which come up for discussion sometimes call for formal resolutions covering legal matters, such as the execution of a mortgage or the release of property, or things of that kind. That is just a normal, ordinary resolution and it says "Resolved that the company agrees to do thus and so". Now, there is nothing formalized in bylaws about that. They proceed in the ordinary way any board of directors proceeds. There is, as I say, a public list of bylaws which refer to the conduct of the public in respect of company property, trespassing, spitting on the platform, committing nuisances on trains, and things of that kind.

I will not continue. My hon. friend and my colleague have enough. There are no bylaws governing the meetings of the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways. Those meetings take place haphazardly according to the wish of Mr. Gordon.
I want my hon. friend to realize that I have observed the most parliamentary language in respect of this matter and that a suggestion or criticism is not an offence. I am sure that my hon. friend is not offended by what I have said to him. Mr. Gordon had no reason to be offended when I made a similar suggestion to him. But he does not accept any suggestion from anyone. So much is that so that we had this incident one day in the committee when reference was made to someone who could have disagreed with him. I said, "You would have fired him at once if he had disagreed with you". He then used an expression which is used in duelling, namely touche; and he happened to be.
The Ottawa Journal which belongs to the same political faith as does the hon. member for York West wrote an editorial on April 29. They headed the editorial, "Donald Gordon No 'Czar' ", It reads in part as follows:
If Mr. Pouliot had more experience of the facts, circumstances and processes which make a corporation or business tick he wouldn't talk such nonsense.
In other words, I would not say that Mr. Gordon could not be at the same time president and chairman of the railway, but I say that for the very good reason that the railway is not like an ordinary corporation, a bank or industry of some kind where the stock is owned by the shareholders and the shareholders meet to elect their directors who represent private interests. In the case of Mr. Gordon of the C.N.R. it is not a matter of private interests. It is public interest because the stock is owned by the people of Canada, and that is why Gordon has to be checked. Otherwise we will have much to complain about him, the same as happened with Sir Henry Thornton. It is very unfortunate. I do not say that to be unpleasant to Gordon. I have no grouch about him, but on the other hand the time has come when parliament should put its nose in that business contrary to the suggestion of the Journal. The editorial goes on:
He would know, to begin with, that Mr. Gordon, as president of the Canadian National and chairman of its board, isn't some sort of czar or mogul issuing edicts right and left to servile trembling subordinates, but mostly one member of a board, largely taking the advice, and sometimes compelled to take the advice, of his executives and fellow directors.
They are all experts over there. If the hon. member for York West (Mr. Hamilton)

knew more about it he would not have spoken as he has done, because I consider him an honest and straightforward colleague. It is a case where ignorance is bliss. The Journal goes on to say:
And Mr. Gordon, in this position, is on all fours with the head or president of any corporation-
It is untrue.
-be it a railway, a bank, an insurance company or a big manufacturing industry.
It is untrue for the reason already mentioned.
In certain circumstances, of course, where there may be lack of unanimity among board members or executives-
There is no lack of unanimity. They are not consulted. It is well known that there cannot be any lack of unanimity because Gordon decides alone.
-it is up to the president or chairman of the board to make a decision; to give the leadership which is implied by his position. But that is far different from his being a dictator, the sole voice or arbiter in all that concerns operation. No corporation could be run in that way-
Well, after having said that I was wrong the conclusion is that I was right, although they do not give me credit for it.
-nor any other institution for that matter. Not any more than it could be run by a babel of voices without some voice in the end having a final say.
This is the most illogical article that has ever been published by the Ottawa Journal, but I am happy with the conclusion. I am thankful for that just the same as I was thankful to my hon. friend for some of the statements he made which confirm my statement. I think if I read fast I will have the satisfaction of putting on record this editorial from the Sydney Post-Record, of April 28, another Tory paper. The Journal is Conservative, the Post-Record is Tory, the two shades of opinion of the Conservative party. The editorial is headed, "Job With Authority", and reads:
A Liberal member of parliament protests that Donald Gordon is too much of a dominant force in running the Canadian National Railways. Mr. Gordon is C.N.R. president-a big man doing a huge job. Canadians certainly do not want a weakling at that post. The accusation of Jean-Frangois Pouliot is frivolous although he himself is in earnest about it.
Thank you, Sydney Post!
His complaint is funny but also a little disturbing. The mighty C.N.R., spanning the continent, with a far-flung network of branching lines,
Canadian National Railways
has the attributes of the circulatory system of a living creature-which it is in the functions it performs, supplying the lifeblood of this young giant of a nation. The C.N.R., the property of Canada, is too vital to the country to be made the plaything of politics. It must have strong and authoritative management.
That is the same thing as my hon. friend has said, the same thing as the Journal has said, the same thing as all Tories everywhere are advocating now and have advocated from the time of Arthur Meighen, Borden, Bennett, Mackenzie and Mann and all those fellows. My young friend said I would like to see the founder of the C.C.F., Mr. Woods-worth, in the gallery, that he would have been proud of that. I will tell him I would have liked to see Arthur Meighen in the gallery. He would have cheered and the Speaker would have had to call him to order. He would have been elated to hear the hon. gentleman. We do not know whether the spirits of Sir Robert Borden and Lord Bennett in the great beyond are not rejoicing with him over his statement. Mackenzie and Mann must be very happy with his speech. I must finish before ten o'clock. The editorial continues:
No one is accusing Donald Gordon of inefficiency or laxness on the job. Instead it appears there are a few complaints in the House of Commons because he is doing it "too well". That's what it amounts to when we analyze what was said. Mr. Gordon simply is making an effective fist of the job he was appointed to do, without political interference but accountable in his performance to the nation.-
But not to the committee. No one can know the price of fence posts.
-And Canadians at large-this seems certain- don't want any political monkeyshines interfering with the job.
Monkeyshines! We are monkeyshines according to this Tory sheet of Sydney. Members of parliament are insulted because they forget-
